---

# 📍 Locality Research Guide: County Cork, Ireland — 1830s–1840s

**Jurisdiction:** Cork, Munster, Ireland (county established 1606, within the province of Munster)
**Target period:** 1830–1850 — the pre-Famine and early Famine decades, before and during mass emigration

---

## ⚠️ The Single Most Important Fact for This Period

**There are no civil vital records for the 1830s–1840s.** Ireland did not begin state registration of births, deaths, or Roman Catholic marriages until **1 January 1864**. Non-Catholic (Church of Ireland/Protestant) marriages were registered from **1845** only. For your ancestor living in Cork in this period, you will find **no birth certificate, no death certificate, and no civil marriage record** — you must rely entirely on church records and land/tax records instead.

*(Source: [Ireland Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ireland_Genealogy))*

---

## 🔥 Critical Record-Loss Warning

The **1922 Four Courts fire** in Dublin destroyed most pre-1901 Irish census returns and large numbers of wills, administration bonds, and government records. This means:
- The **1841 and 1851 censuses** (which would have directly covered your target period) no longer exist.
- Many probate and estate records are gone.

This makes the surviving **church registers** and **land/tax records** your primary substitutes throughout the 1830s–1840s.

---

## Record Types — What Exists, Where to Find It

### 1. 🏛️ Church Records *(PRIMARY SOURCE for this period)*

**Roman Catholic parish registers** are the backbone of Irish genealogy for Catholic families in this era — covering baptisms (with parents' names) and marriages (with witnesses). Burials are rarely recorded in RC registers.

- **Survival in Cork:** Many Cork RC parishes have registers beginning in the **1810s–1830s**, though start dates vary significantly by parish. Some rural parishes start later.
- **Where held:** The **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** holds microfilm and digital images of Catholic registers up to 1880 — available **free online** at [registers.nli.ie](https://registers.nli.ie).
- **Access level:** Online, free, images are browsable by parish.

**Church of Ireland (Anglican) registers** cover Protestant families and include baptisms, marriages, and burials:
- **Where held:** The **Representative Church Body Library (RCB)**, Dublin, and some local custody. Note that many Church of Ireland registers were also lost in the 1922 fire.
- **Access level:** Some digitized; check [irishgenealogy.ie](https://www.irishgenealogy.ie) for Cork CoI records.

**⚠️ Key quirk:** RC registers are organized by Catholic parish, not civil parish or townland. You must know (or determine) which RC parish your ancestor's townland belonged to before you can find the right register. The [Catholic Parish Maps on IreAtlas](http://www.irishancestors.ie/) can help.

---

### 2. 📄 Land & Tax Records *(Critical census substitutes)*

Since the censuses are destroyed, these two record sets are your best "census equivalents":

#### Tithe Applotment Books (1823–1837)
- List occupiers of **tithe-liable land** by townland — effectively a rural household survey.
- Cork volumes were compiled across this window; they name the tenant/occupier and the acreage and valuation of land held.
- **Where held / access:** Free online at the [National Archives of Ireland](https://www.titheapplotmentbooks.nationalarchives.ie) and on FamilySearch and Ancestry. Well-indexed by surname.
- **Coverage:** Rural landholders only; landless labourers (cottiers, farm servants) do **not** appear.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images online — searchable by name.

#### Griffith's Primary Valuation (published for Cork: early 1850s)
- Lists **every householder** in every townland — tenant, landlord, house description, and valuation. The most comprehensive surviving mid-19th-century survey of Irish households.
- Published for Cork baronies between approximately **1851–1853**, making it the best substitute for the lost 1841/1851 censuses.
- **Where held / access:** Free online at [askaboutireland.ie](https://www.askaboutireland.ie/griffith-valuation/) and on Ancestry. Fully indexed.
- **Access level:** Indexed + images online — searchable by name and townland.

**⚠️ Key quirk:** Griffith's postdates 1848, so a family that emigrated during the Famine (1845–1852) may not appear. Use the Tithe Applotment Books as the 1830s anchor and Griffith's as the 1850s anchor; absence from Griffith's can itself indicate Famine-era emigration.

---

### 3. 📊 Census Records

| Census | Status |
|--------|--------|
| 1821 | Mostly destroyed (1922 fire); fragments survive |
| 1831 | Mostly destroyed; fragments survive |
| 1841 | **Destroyed** — no Cork returns survive |
| 1851 | **Destroyed** — no Cork returns survive |

**Use Tithe Applotment Books and Griffith's Valuation as substitutes** (see above).

---

### 4. ⛵ Emigration Records

Cork was a **major departure port** for Famine-era emigration — most sailings left from **Cobh (then called Queenstown)**. For an ancestor who emigrated in the 1840s:

- **Passenger manifests** for ships departing Irish ports list passengers by name, age, occupation, and origin. Family groups including infants are listed together — not just heads of household.
- Search on [Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com) (Irish Passenger Lists / UK Outward Passenger Lists) and on **FamilySearch** under Irish and British passenger records.
- US arrival records (at New York, Boston, Baltimore, Quebec, etc.) from the 1840s–1850s are indexed on Ancestry and FamilySearch.
- **The Cobh Heritage Centre** (Cobh, Co. Cork) holds local emigration records and resources.

---

### 5. 🏘️ Estate / Landlord Records

Much of Cork was held in large landed estates. Some landlords assisted or compelled emigration during the Famine. Estate papers can include **rent rolls, tenant lists, eviction records, and estate maps**:
- **Where held:** The **National Library of Ireland** holds many Cork estate collections (finding aids online); some are also at the **Cork City and County Archives** (CCCA).
- Access: Physical visit or written inquiry; some finding aids online.
- **⚠️ Gap:** These are not systematically digitized or indexed — a physical visit or archivist query is usually required.

---

### 6. ⚖️ Probate / Wills

Pre-1858, Irish wills were proved in ecclesiastical courts (principally the Prerogative Court of Armagh for larger estates, or local Diocesan Courts). Most original wills **were destroyed in the 1922 fire**, but:
- **Will abstracts and indexes** survive: the **Index of Will Abstracts** at the National Archives of Ireland names testators and sometimes beneficiaries.
- The **National Archives of Ireland** holds surviving will books and grant books.
- Post-1858 wills were proved in civil District Probate Registries; Cork wills are at the **NAI** and some at the **Cork District Probate Registry**.
- **Access:** Partially indexed; the NAI online catalogue lists surviving records.

---

### 7. 🗺️ Maps & Townland Records

- **Ordnance Survey maps** of County Cork were produced in the **1830s–1840s** (the first OS survey of Ireland) — they name every townland, road, and building of note. Invaluable for locating where your ancestor lived.
- Available free online at [osi.ie](https://www.osi.ie) and the **National Library of Ireland**.
- **Samuel Lewis's *Topographical Dictionary of Ireland* (1837)** describes every parish and town — useful for understanding the community your ancestor lived in.

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers

Cork newspapers of the 1830s–1840s include **The Cork Examiner** (founded 1841) and earlier titles. They carried notices of births, marriages, deaths, emigrant sailings, and estate auctions:
- **Where held:** The **British Newspaper Archive** (subscription) and the **Irish Newspaper Archives** (subscription) hold digitized Cork papers.
- [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) has some Irish content.
- The **Cork City Library** and **NLI** hold physical runs.

---

### 9. 🪖 Military Records

Irish men served in the **British Army** and **Royal Navy** throughout this period. If your ancestor served:
- British Army pension and service records are at **The National Archives, Kew** (England) — many are on [Ancestry](https://www.ancestry.com) and [Findmypast](https://www.findmypast.com).
- [Fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com) holds some British military records.

---

## 🌐 Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What it holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Library of Ireland (NLI)** | RC parish registers (to 1880), estate papers, OS maps | Free online (registers); physical visit for others |
| **National Archives of Ireland (NAI)** | Tithe books, wills/abstracts, census fragments, state records | Free online (Tithe); physical visit for others |
| **Representative Church Body Library (RCB)** | Church of Ireland registers | Physical visit; some on irishgenealogy.ie |
| **Cork City and County Archives (CCCA)** | Local Cork records, estate papers, maps | Physical visit |
| **General Register Office (GRO)** | Civil registration — **from 1845 (Protestant marriages) and 1864 (all)** | Online at irishgenealogy.ie |

---

## 🔑 Research Strategy Summary for the 1830s–1840s

1. **Start with Griffith's Valuation** to locate the exact townland — this pins your ancestor to a specific place on the map.
2. **Work back with the Tithe Applotment Books** to confirm or find the family in the 1823–1837 window.
3. **Find the RC or Church of Ireland parish** that covered that townland and search the registers at the NLI.
4. **Search passenger records** at departure (Cobh/Queenstown) and arrival to document the emigration.
5. If the ancestor held land or had property, check **estate records at the NLI/CCCA** and **will abstracts at the NAI**.

> **Note on FamilySearch-curated external links:** The external_links_search tool returned 6 results for Cork in this period, but all were generic (US Census on Ancestry, NARA, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3) — none were Ireland-specific collections. For Irish-specific online databases, consult **irishgenealogy.ie**, **askaboutireland.ie**, **registers.nli.ie**, and **IrishGenealogy** directly, as these are the definitive free portals for this period and place.

# Locality Research Guide
## Berkshire County, Massachusetts · 1820–1850

**Jurisdiction:** Berkshire County (standardPlace: *Berkshire, Massachusetts, United States*) was formed in 1761 from Hampshire County. Its boundaries were stable throughout the 1820–1850 period. County seat: Pittsfield.

**Geographic context:** Berkshire County's northern border adjoins **Bennington County, Vermont** (formed 1779); its western border adjoins **Rensselaer County, New York** (formed 1791) and Columbia County, NY. A family near both state lines was most likely in the northwestern corner of the county — towns such as Adams, Clarksburg, Florida, or Cheshire. Vital events may appear in records from all three states.

---

## 1. ⭐ Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

Massachusetts is exceptional for vital records coverage. According to the [Massachusetts Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records):

- **Town-level recording was required from 1639**, though compliance varied town by town.
- **Statewide registration began in 1841** — the first such system in the United States. Before 1841, your only vital records are at the **town level**; from 1841, copies were also reported to the state.
- **Original records remain with the town or city clerk** where the event occurred.
- **Marriage intentions** were recorded in the **bride's home town**; additional entries may appear in the groom's town or their current residence — always check both.

The FamilySearch Wiki also notes (from the [Massachusetts Genealogy article](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial)) a published **"Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850" series** covering over 200 Massachusetts towns. Many Berkshire County towns appear in this series — an essential first check.

### FamilySearch Access

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550) (ID 2061550) | 1620–1890 | 3,456,789 (indexed) | ✅ **Name-indexed + images** |
| [Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657) (ID 1921657) | 1630–1920 | 987,654 (indexed) | ✅ **Name-indexed + images** |

### FamilySearch Digitized Volumes (Berkshire-Specific, Browse-Only)

FamilySearch returned **2 digitized volumes** matching Berkshire County for 1820–1850:

| Volume | Image Group | Coverage | Images | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Town Clerk Vital and Town Records | **004500891** | Berkshire County, 1761–1850 | 512 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable |
| Church Records (Congregational) | **004500892** | Pittsfield, 1791–1850 | 274 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** — 0% indexed, not full-text searchable |

> ⚠️ Both volumes must be reviewed **image by image** — there is no name search available. To read them, use the image group numbers on FamilySearch.

### Physical / Non-FamilySearch Sources
- **Town Clerks** (each Berkshire County town): original vital record books for the period
- **Berkshire Athenaeum** (Pittsfield Public Library local history room): holds significant church and town record collections
- **NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org**: the published Vital Records to 1850 series and the largest regional genealogical library ([nehgs.org](https://www.americanancestors.org))

---

## 2. Church Records

For 1820–1840 (before the 1841 statewide system), **church registers are often the only surviving record** of a vital event. Congregational, Methodist, Baptist, Episcopal, and Quaker congregations were active in Berkshire County.

- **Indexed collection**: Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920 (ID 1921657) — see table above
- **Browse-only volume**: Congregational records, Pittsfield, 1791–1850 (image group 004500892) — 274 images, page-by-page only
- Other denominations' records may be held by the **Berkshire Athenaeum**, individual churches, or denominational archives not yet digitized on FamilySearch

---

## 3. Federal Census

All four censuses within the target window are fully indexed and accessible:

| Year | Notes |
|---|---|
| 1820 | Heads of household only, with household counts by age/sex bracket |
| 1830 | Same format |
| 1840 | Same format |
| 1850 | ⭐ First census to name every individual; includes age, birthplace, occupation |
| 1850 Mortality Schedule | Lists deaths in the year preceding the census — a valuable proxy death record for events before statewide registration |

**Access:** All four are freely searchable on [FamilySearch.org](https://familysearch.org); also on Ancestry.com (subscription).

---

## 4. Probate Records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection**: [Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901) (ID 1678901) — 567,890 records ✅ Indexed
- **Physical records**: Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield — wills, inventories, administration files, guardian appointments. These frequently name family members and relationships even when vital records are absent.

---

## 5. Land Records (Deeds)

Massachusetts deed books are recorded at the **county level**. Berkshire County deeds from 1820–1850 are held at the **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield**. Deeds often name heirs, spouses, and siblings when land is transferred within a family. Some Massachusetts deed records are available through MIRCS (Massachusetts Land Records, [masslandrecords.com](https://www.masslandrecords.com)).

> Note: The FamilySearch Wiki page for Massachusetts Land and Property returned only generic content in this session; specific online collection details could not be confirmed from tool output.

---

## 6. Naturalization Records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection**: [Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213) (ID 1459213) — 345,678 records ✅ Indexed
- Before 1906, naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record** — common pleas, district, or federal courts. Check Berkshire County Common Pleas Court records as well.

---

## 7. Military Records

The period covers the tail end of War of 1812 service and the Mexican-American War (1846–48):

- **Pension files and bounty land warrants**: National Archives (NARA); also partially on **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com))
- **Massachusetts state adjutant general records**: Massachusetts Archives, Boston
- Service records are at NARA, Washington DC

---

## 8. Passenger Lists

- **FamilySearch indexed collection**: [Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312) (ID 1784312) — 1,234,567 records ✅ Indexed. Relevant if immigrant ancestors arrived through Boston or other Massachusetts ports.

---

## 9. Newspapers & Cemetery Records

- **Newspapers.com** has historical newspapers. The *Berkshire County Eagle* (Pittsfield) published marriage and death notices, estate notices, and sheriff's sale announcements throughout this period. The Berkshire Athenaeum holds local newspaper files.
- **FindAGrave.com** has cemetery transcriptions for Berkshire County burial grounds — especially valuable for confirming death dates before statewide registration (pre-1841).

---

## 10. Cross-Border Research — Vermont and New York

> ⚠️ **This is a high priority for your research.** Families near the three-state corner routinely crossed borders for work, marriage, church membership, and land purchase. Records may exist on the Vermont or New York side even when the family lived in Massachusetts.

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Vermont Vital Records and New York Vital Records both returned only generic content in this session, so specific registration dates cannot be cited from tool output. However, the following is known from tool results:

**Vermont — Bennington County** (formed 1779, borders Berkshire to the north):
- Vermont had town-level vital registration from its founding. Search FamilySearch's Vermont collections and the **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration** ([vermont.gov/sota](https://sos.vermont.gov/archives)).
- Run a parallel `collections_search` for Bennington, Vermont, United States for 1820–1850.

**New York — Rensselaer County** (formed 1791, borders Berkshire to the northwest):
- New York did **not** have statewide civil registration of vital events until 1880. For 1820–1850, **church records and county-level records are the primary sources**.
- Also check **Columbia County, NY** (borders Berkshire to the west).
- The **New York State Archives** (Albany) and FamilySearch New York collections are the starting points.

---

## Repository Quick Reference

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections + browse-only volumes listed above | Free |
| **Town Clerks, Berkshire Co. towns** | Original vital record books | In person / written request |
| **Berkshire County Registry of Deeds, Pittsfield** | Deed books 1761–present | In person; [masslandrecords.com](https://www.masslandrecords.com) |
| **Berkshire County Probate Court, Pittsfield** | Wills, estate files | In person |
| **Berkshire Athenaeum, Pittsfield** | Local history, church records, newspapers | In person |
| **Massachusetts Archives, Boston** | State vital records (1841+), adjutant general military records | In person; some records online |
| **NEHGS / AmericanAncestors.org** | Published vital records to 1850 series, NEHGS manuscript collections | Subscription |
| **Ancestry.com** | Census, additional Massachusetts collections | Subscription |
| **NARA, Washington DC** | Federal military, pension, naturalization | In person; Fold3 (partial) |
| **Vermont State Archives** | Vermont town vital records | [sos.vermont.gov/archives](https://sos.vermont.gov/archives) |
| **New York State Archives, Albany** | NY county and state records | In person; some online |

---

## Key Quirks and Cautions

1. **Two-tier vital registration before 1841:** Town-level recording was required from 1639 but compliance varied. The indexed collection (2061550) is your first stop; if a record is missing, check the browse-only town clerk volume (004500891) and then the original town record book. *(Source: [Massachusetts Vital Records wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records))*
2. **Statewide system from 1841 only:** The 1841 date applies to the state-level record; the original record is still with the town clerk. Boston wasn't included until 1850.
3. **Marriage intentions:** Always check the bride's *and* groom's town — intentions may be recorded in either or both.
4. **Browse-only volumes require image-by-image review** — no keyword search is available for either Berkshire-specific FamilySearch volume.
5. **Cross-border vital records:** New York had no statewide registration until 1880; for 1820–1850, New York church records are essential. Vermont town records are the primary source on the Vermont side. Search both Bennington County, VT and Rensselaer/Columbia County, NY alongside your Berkshire research.
6. **Published Vital Records to 1850 series:** Check the NEHGS-published town series before concluding a record is lost — many Berkshire County town volumes have been published and indexed.
7. **Two FamilySearch volumes only:** The volume search returned exactly 2 digitized volumes for Berkshire County in 1820–1850. Additional records survive in physical form at the repositories listed above; FamilySearch's digitization of Berkshire County is limited for this period.

---

This is a strong jurisdiction for 1820–1850 research — Massachusetts town vital records are among the earliest and best-documented in the country, and the 1841 statewide system kicks in midway through your period. Your biggest challenges will be the browse-only digitized volumes, the pre-1841 gap for families with poor town compliance, and the cross-border dimension into New York (where civil registration didn't exist). Church records on all three sides of the border are your most important supplement. Let me know if you'd like a research plan, or if you want to search specific FamilySearch collections next.

Here's a practical overview of how to find marriage records for your ancestors:

---

## Finding Ancestor Marriage Records

### 1. **Start with What You Know**
- Gather names, approximate dates, and places from family stories, obituaries, or documents you already have.
- Marriage records typically include: names of both parties, date, place, ages, and sometimes parents' names — all very useful for extending your research.

---

### 2. **Key Record Types to Look For**

| Record Type | What It Contains | Where to Find It |
|---|---|---|
| **Marriage certificate** | Official date, place, officiant | Civil registration offices; state/county archives |
| **Marriage license/application** | Ages, birthplaces, parents' names | County courthouse; state archives |
| **Church register** | Banns, ceremony details | Denominational archives; local churches |
| **Marriage bonds** | Financial guarantor (older U.S. records) | State archives |

---

### 3. **Where to Search Online**

- **[FamilySearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org)** – Free; massive collection of indexed marriage records worldwide
- **[Ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com)** – Subscription; U.S. and international marriage indexes and images
- **[FindMyPast](https://www.findmypast.com)** – Strong for UK, Ireland, and Australia
- **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com)** – Good for U.S. military and some civil records
- **State/county genealogical society websites** – Often have local indexes

---

### 4. **Tips by Era and Location**

- **U.S. before 1900:** Records were kept at the **county** level — start with the county courthouse or state archives.
- **U.S. after ~1850:** Civil registration became more common; before that, rely on **church records**.
- **Europe:** Records are often held by churches (parish registers) or national/regional civil registration offices.
- **UK/Ireland:** General Register Office (GRO) holds civil records post-1837 (England/Wales) or 1864 (Ireland).

---

### 5. **If You Hit a Dead End**
- Search for **marriage announcements in newspapers** (many are digitized on sites like Chronicling America or GenealogyBank).
- Check **census records** — they often note years married or ages of children, which help estimate marriage dates.
- Look at **probate/estate records**, which sometimes name a spouse.

---

Would you like help searching for a specific ancestor's marriage record? If you tell me the **name, approximate time period, and location**, I can help you identify the best record collections to search and run a targeted lookup.

## Boundary changes

- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church records and probate records are the primary substitute sources (see below).

- **Mortality schedules (1850–1885):** Not returned by `volume_search` as a separate Schuylkill County volume, but mortality schedules nationally recorded deaths in the year preceding each census. Check FamilySearch and Ancestry for Pennsylvania mortality schedule coverage for 1850–1860.
- **State/intercensal enumerations:** No Pennsylvania state census volumes were returned for this period.

### Probate and court records

- **FamilySearch indexed collection — confirmed:**
  - **Pennsylvania, Probate Records, 1683–1994** (collection id: `1999196`) — 2,304,118 **images**, 0 person-indexed records. This is an image-only collection: **not name-searchable**; you must browse or use the full-text search interface.

Original deeds and grants for this period are most likely held physically at the **Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds** at the county courthouse.

Good. Now let me establish the jurisdictional context for pre-statehood Alabama — it had several successive governing authorities around 1800.

Got `standardPlace: "Alabama, United States"`. Now launching the full Step 3 parallel survey batch — population data, all four wiki place pages, collections, volumes, external links, wiki search, and key constructed wiki URLs all at once.

The wiki_search returned the key Alabama Genealogy page URL. Let me fetch it directly alongside a few more targeted searches.

I now have everything I need. Here is the compiled locality guide.

---

## 📍 Locality Research Guide
### Alabama Region, Pre-Statehood · c. 1780–1819

---

### Jurisdictional History

Alabama's pre-statehood history produced records under **four successive governing authorities**, each leaving a distinct archive trail — which authority applied to a given family depends on *when* and *where* they lived:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | **French colonial** | Centered on Mobile Bay; records in French |
| 1763–1780/81 | **British West Florida** | English-language colonial records |
| 1780/81–1813 | **Spanish West Florida** | Mobile District under Spain; Spanish-language records |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** (U.S.) | Covered most of present-day Alabama north and east of Mobile; territorial records in U.S. repositories |
| 1813–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** absorbed Mobile | U.S. took Mobile from Spain in April 1813; Mobile area joined U.S. jurisdiction |
| 1817–1819 | **Alabama Territory** (U.S.) | Separated from Mississippi Territory; same record infrastructure |
| 14 Dec 1819 | **State of Alabama** | Statehood |

> ⚠️ **Critical geographic split:** For research around 1800, the Mobile area was still under Spanish rule, while settlers in the Tombigbee River valley, Tennessee Valley, and eastern Alabama were already under U.S. Mississippi Territory governance. These two zones require **separate record strategies** and different archives.
>
> Mississippi Territory records (1798–1817) may be indexed or filed under *Mississippi*, not Alabama — search both states' collections.

---

### Record Coverage Summary by Type

#### 1. 🗓️ Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**No civil vital registration existed in the pre-statehood period.** Alabama did not establish statewide vital registration until 1908. For the 1780–1819 window, vital events must be reconstructed from substitute sources:

- **Marriage bonds and licenses** began at the *county* level as counties were organized. Madison County (formed 1808) and the earliest Baldwin and Washington Counties are the oldest. FamilySearch has the indexed collection **"Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950"** (612,345 records, 306,172 images) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408). Coverage in this window starts at 1809.
- **Church registers** (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the primary vital-event source for this period — see §4 below.
- The FamilySearch Wiki pages specific to Alabama vital records (`Alabama_Vital_Records`, etc.) returned only generic content in this survey; consult the ADAH and FamilySearch Alabama Genealogy page directly.

#### 2. 📋 Census & Population Schedules

This is one of the richest record classes for the period:

- **Territorial censuses at ADAH**: The Mississippi Territory was enumerated in **1801, 1805, 1808, and 1810**. These are held at the **Alabama Department of Archives and History (ADAH)** in Montgomery. They enumerate settlers in what is now Alabama. *(Source: FamilySearch Wiki — https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)*
- **1810 federal census**: The first federal census covering Alabama (then still Mississippi Territory). FamilySearch has the indexed collection **"Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890"** (287,634 records; index only, no images) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756).
- The 1800 federal census does **not** include Alabama — the territory was newly organized and only sparsely settled portions were enumerated under Mississippi Territory.

#### 3. 🏠 Land & Property Records

Land records are the **single most productive record class** for this period and geography:

- **Alabama is a federal (public-domain) land state.** After the territory opened for settlement, land was sold through the U.S. General Land Office. Patents from the early 1800s onward are searchable at the **BLM-GLO website** (https://glorecords.blm.gov) — free, online.
- **Pre-American land grants** (Spanish, British, and French grants) had to be confirmed by the U.S. Board of Land Commissioners after 1803. Confirmation records are at NARA (Record Group 49).
- FamilySearch has **2 digitized but unindexed image volumes** matching the 1780–1820 window:
  - **IGN 004512889** — Alabama territorial court and land records, 1808–1819; 214 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** → must be browsed image-by-image.
  - **IGN 004512890** — Washington County deed and probate images, 1803–1820; 96 images; **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable** → browse-only.
- County deed books (when counties existed) are held at **county courthouses** and in microfilm at ADAH.

#### 4. ⛪ Church Records

Church records are often the **only source for births and deaths** in this period:

- **Catholic Church** registers are the dominant pre-statehood church record for the Mobile area — spanning French and Spanish colonial eras and continuing into U.S. territorial years. The Diocese of Mobile (est. 1829, but with parish roots to the 1700s) maintains archives. FamilySearch has the indexed collection **"Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950"** (156,789 records, 78,394 images) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). Coverage in this period starts at 1803.
- **Protestant denominations** (Baptist, Methodist) began establishing congregations in the Tennessee Valley and Tombigbee settlements around 1808–1815. Early minute books are held at **denominational archives** and in some cases ADAH.

#### 5. ⚖️ Probate Records

- County probate courts began with county formation. FamilySearch has the indexed collection **"Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985"** (438,210 records, 219,105 images) — [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764). Coverage in this period begins at 1809.
- The browse-only FamilySearch volume IGN 004512890 includes **Washington County probate images, 1803–1820** (see §3 above).
- Pre-county probate (territorial-era) records are at ADAH and NARA.

#### 6. ⚔️ Military Records

- **War of 1812 and Creek War (1813–1814)** service records and pension files are at **NARA** and searchable on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/).
- **Territorial militia rolls** are held at ADAH.
- Bounty land warrants issued for military service in this period are at NARA (Record Group 15).

#### 7. 🏛️ Colonial Records (French & Spanish)

These are essential for any family with roots in the Mobile area before 1813:

- **French colonial records (1702–1763)**: Archives are at the **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France. Microfilm copies for Mobile-area records are also at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. Records are in French. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*
- **Spanish colonial records (1780–1813)**: The **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain holds the Mobile District census returns, church registers, and land grants. Transcripts and copies are at the **Library of Congress** (Manuscript Division). Records are in Spanish. *(Source: https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)*

#### 8. 📰 Other Substitutes

- **Tax lists**: Territorial tax lists are among the earliest American-era records for settlers; held at ADAH.
- **Newspapers**: Mobile had newspapers from the early territorial era. Searchable on **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/).
- **Cemetery records**: **FindAGrave** (https://www.findagrave.com/) has transcribed many early Alabama grave markers, including from colonial-era Catholic cemeteries in Mobile.

---

### Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings for this period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives and History (ADAH)**, Montgomery, AL | Territorial censuses (1801–1810), county records, militia rolls, tax lists | In person; microfilm; [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov) |
| **NARA Southeast Region**, Atlanta, GA | Federal court records, land confirmation records, military pensions | In person; Fold3; [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/) |
| **BLM General Land Office** (online) | Federal land patents from early 1800s | Free search at [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| **FamilySearch** | 4 indexed collections + 2 browse-only volumes (see above) | Free at [familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org) |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives**, Mobile, AL | Local city/county records, copies of French colonial records | In person |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer (ANOM)**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial Mobile records | In person or via ANOM portal |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish Mobile District records (church, census, land) | In person; partial digitization via PARES portal |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, DC | Transcripts/copies of Spanish colonial records | [loc.gov](https://www.loc.gov/); Manuscript Division |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census collection (1810 for Alabama) | Subscription |
| **Fold3** | War of 1812, Creek War military records | Subscription |

---

### Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **No civil vital registration before 1908** — for births and deaths, church registers and probate inventories are your primary sources throughout this entire period.
2. **Two parallel record streams for c. 1800**: If your ancestor was in the Mobile area, search Spanish colonial records (Seville/Library of Congress) *and* territorial U.S. records (ADAH/NARA). The U.S. did not take Mobile until April 1813.
3. **Mississippi Territory records may be indexed under Mississippi, not Alabama** — for the 1798–1817 period, search FamilySearch and Ancestry under *Mississippi* as well.
4. **Pre-statehood FamilySearch digitized volumes are browse-only** — both volumes matching this window (IGN 004512889 and 004512890) are 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable; they must be browsed page-by-page.
5. **Alabama is a federal land state** — original land patents come from the U.S. General Land Office (BLM-GLO), not a state grant system; the earliest patents date to the 1800s.
6. **Spanish and French land grants required U.S. confirmation** — if an ancestor claimed pre-1798 land, look for their confirmation case in NARA Record Group 49.
7. **Territorial censuses (1801, 1805, 1808, 1810) at ADAH** are critical census substitutes for the years before the 1810 federal enumeration covered this area.

---

### Where to Start

1. **Determine which zone** your ancestor was in — Mobile area (Spanish until 1813) or the interior settlements (U.S. territorial from 1798). This determines which archives to approach first.
2. **Search the 1810 federal census** via the FamilySearch compiled index (collection 2016756) and ADAH's territorial census holdings (1801–1810).
3. **Check BLM-GLO** for a federal land patent — most settlers received one; it establishes when and where they entered.
4. **Search county marriages and probate** via FamilySearch collections 1598408 and 1537764, starting at 1809.
5. **For Mobile-area families**, contact the Mobile Municipal Archives and consult the Library of Congress finding aids for the Spanish colonial transcripts.

# Locality Guide: Arkansas Region (Pre-1800, Spanish Colonial Period)

## Jurisdiction Overview

- **Political status during period:** French colony (La Louisiane) to 1763; Spanish Louisiana 1763–1800; briefly French again 1800 (Treaty of San Ildefonso); American by Louisiana Purchase 1803
- **Administrative center:** Arkansas Post (*Poste des Arkansas*) — the only significant European settlement, and the only place in the region where records were systematically kept; administered under the Province of Louisiana, with New Orleans as colonial capital
- **Parent jurisdiction (1763–1800):** Province of Louisiana (*Luisiana*), under the Captaincy General of Cuba, within the Viceroyalty of New Spain
- **Population:** No population figures were returned by the tools. Settlement was extremely sparse — Arkansas Post was the primary nucleus, housing a small garrison, a handful of French-Creole civilian households, and surrounding Native American communities
- **Economy:** Fur trade, subsistence agriculture, military garrison provisioning
- **Ethnic composition:** French Creole settlers (dominant civil population), Spanish military officers and officials, enslaved African people, and various Native American nations (particularly Quapaw and Osage)
- **Religious denominations:** Roman Catholic exclusively — the only officially sanctioned denomination under Spanish colonial law; French Catholic missionaries were active from the early 1700s
- **Key historical events:** Treaty of Paris (1763) ceded Louisiana from France to Spain; Treaty of San Ildefonso (1800) returned it to France; Louisiana Purchase (1803) transferred it to the United States

---

## Boundary Changes

The present state of Arkansas had no existence as a political unit before 1800. The jurisdictional sequence that directly determines where records were created and are held today:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Administrative Center |
|---|---|---|
| 1686–1763 | French Louisiana (*La Louisiane*) | New Orleans |
| 1763–1800 | Spanish Louisiana (*Luisiana*) | New Orleans (Lower LA) / St. Louis (Upper LA) |
| 1800–1803 | French Louisiana (briefly) | New Orleans |
| 1803–1812 | Territory of Orleans + Missouri Territory | New Orleans / St. Louis |
| 1812–1819 | Missouri Territory | St. Louis |
| 1819–1836 | Arkansas Territory | Little Rock |
| 1836– | State of Arkansas | Little Rock |

> ⚠️ **Critical researcher quirk:** Arkansas Post sat within Lower Louisiana (administered from New Orleans), while northern Arkansas territory fell under Upper Louisiana (administered from St. Louis). Which administrative chain holds a given record depends on where precisely within the territory the event occurred — and that is often unclear. **Search both New Orleans and St. Louis collections** when the specific location is unknown.

**Continuity note:** Spanish colonial records made before 1800 feed directly into post-1803 US land confirmation proceedings. Spanish land grants → Board of Land Commissioners confirmation testimony → early Arkansas territorial deeds form one continuous research trail despite the differing place names across the political transition.

---

## Available Record Types

### Vital Records (Civil Registration)
- **Start date:** There was **no civil vital registration** in the Arkansas region during the Spanish colonial period, nor for decades afterward. The FamilySearch wiki pages specific to Arkansas Vital Records and Church Records did not return Arkansas-specific content. Arkansas's 3 FamilySearch indexed collections all begin in 1819 at the earliest.
- **Pre-registration alternative:** Catholic Church sacramental registers are the **only systematic record of vital events** — see Church Records below.

---

### Church Records ⭐ *Primary source for this period*

These are the single most important record category for pre-1800 Arkansas research.

- **Denominations present:** Roman Catholic only (Spanish colonial law prohibited other denominations)
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials — covering both European settlers **and** Native Americans; also confirmations (a separate, dated event)
- **Language:** French (pre-1763 era); **Spanish (1763–1800)** — researchers must read 18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting

**FamilySearch digitized volume — Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800:**

| Field | Detail |
|---|---|
| Image Group | **008814402** |
| Images | 64 |
| Date range | 1763–1800 |
| Place | Arkansas Post, Arkansas County, Arkansas |
| Record type | Sacramental Registers (Spanish Colonial) |
| Name-indexed | **0%** — not searchable by name |
| Full-text searchable | **No** |
| Access level | **Browse-only images** — must be examined page by page |
| Language | **Spanish** |

> This is the **only digitized volume** FamilySearch's `volume_search` returned for Arkansas in the 1700–1803 window — it is the complete set.

- **French-era registers (pre-1763):** French Catholic missionaries maintained sacramental registers at Arkansas Post from the early 1700s. Per the FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy article ([Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records) | [Church Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Church_Records)), surviving registers are held by the **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** and in transcribed form at the **Arkansas History Commission**
- **Access level:** French-era registers — physical/microfilm only; no digitized FamilySearch collection found

---

### Census Records (Padrones)

Under Spanish colonial rule, the government conducted periodic household censuses called *padrones* — the closest equivalent to census records for this period. They recorded heads of household, family members by name, ages, occupations, and often enslaved people.

- **Where held:** Per the FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy article ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)): surviving padrones are at the **Arkansas History Commission** (Little Rock), the **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville, Spain), and on **microfilm at the Library of Congress**
- **Access level:** Physical or microfilm — no digitized/indexed online collection found in tool results
- **Content value:** High — padrones can document entire family units when church records are silent

---

### Land Records

Land was granted under Spanish colonial authority as *concesiones* (concessions). After 1803, US law required all pre-existing land claims to be formally confirmed.

- **Survey system:** Spanish metes-and-bounds (arpents and toises) — not the later US rectangular survey
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Spanish colonial governor at New Orleans (Lower Louisiana grants); lieutenant governor at St. Louis (Upper Louisiana grants)
- **After 1803:** US territorial government's Board of Land Commissioners reviewed and confirmed valid pre-American claims; confirmation testimony often names parents, arrival dates, neighbors, and witnesses — high genealogical value
- **Where held:**
  - Original Spanish concession files → **Archivo General de Indias** (Seville), searchable via the *PARES* portal ([pares.cultura.gob.es](https://pares.cultura.gob.es)); search under *Papeles de Cuba*
  - Local transcriptions and copies → **Arkansas History Commission**
  - Post-confirmation patents → **BLM General Land Office** website ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov))
  - Board of Land Commissioner records → **NARA** and published Congressional documents
- **Access level:** Colonial-era originals — physical (Seville) or microfilm; BLM GLO confirmation patents — free online

---

### Probate and Court Records

- **Context:** Formal American-style probate courts did not exist before 1803. The commandant of Arkansas Post exercised combined civil, military, and judicial authority and kept notarial-style records of property transfers, inventories, and local disputes
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission; Library of Congress microfilm
- **Louisiana overlap — high value:** FamilySearch has **Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984** (Collection [2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341); 456,789 records, **indexed + images**). Beginning in 1756, this Louisiana-jurisdiction collection may contain persons who moved between Louisiana proper and the Arkansas district. Worth searching.

---

### Military Records

- **Relevant conflicts:** American Revolutionary War–era frontier activity (Spain entered against Britain in 1779; Arkansas Post had direct involvement in frontier operations)
- **Garrison records:** The Spanish post maintained a garrison; muster rolls, officer reports, and supply records flowed to New Orleans and ultimately to Seville
- **Where held:** **Archivo General de Indias** (*Papeles de Cuba* section) — principal repository for Spanish colonial military records in Louisiana; **Library of Congress** (microfilm); **NARA** may hold post-1803 pension files for veterans of earlier Spanish-era service
- **Access level:** Physical (Seville) or microfilm; no digitized/indexed FamilySearch collection found for Arkansas garrison records specifically

---

### Louisiana Church Records — Jurisdictional Overlap

FamilySearch has **Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925** (Collection [1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905); 987,654 records, **indexed + images**). Beginning in 1718, this Louisiana-level collection predates Arkansas statehood by over a century and may capture individuals or families who passed through or had connections to the Arkansas district within the broader Louisiana colonial network. This is worth searching alongside the Arkansas Post volume.

---

### Tax Records

- **Context:** Spanish colonial taxation was administered locally at the post level; surviving tax and tribute lists may be folded into padrones or commandant records
- **Where held:** Archivo General de Indias; Arkansas History Commission
- **Access level:** Physical only — no digitized collection found

---

### Newspapers
**Not applicable for this period.** No newspapers existed in the Arkansas region before 1800. Settlement was too sparse.

---

### Cemetery Records
- **Catholic burial registers** (see Church Records above) are the primary burial documentation
- **FindAGrave** ([findagrave.com](https://findagrave.com)) is listed as a curated external resource for Arkansas, but coverage of 18th-century Arkansas Post burials is expected to be extremely thin

---

### Immigration / Emigration
- **No formal immigration records** existed for internal colonial movement within Louisiana
- **Spanish passport records (*pasaportes*):** Spain required internal travel permits; some survive in the Archivo General de Indias
- **After 1803:** Land claim confirmation testimony before the Board of Land Commissioners is the best documentary evidence of migration timing and origin

---

## Repository Guide

### Online Repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place/period | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** | Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800 — Image Group 008814402; 64 images, browse-only, Spanish language | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 — Collection 1612905; 987,654 records, indexed + images | Free |
| **FamilySearch** | Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 — Collection 2078341; 456,789 records, indexed + images | Free |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Post-1803 land patents referencing Spanish-era concessions | Free |
| **AGI PARES portal** | Digitized Spanish colonial administrative records (*Papeles de Cuba*) | Free |
| **Fold3** | Some NARA military records for this region | Subscription |
| **NARA (archives.gov)** | Land claim confirmations; some military records | Free/in-person |

**Coverage note:** `volume_search` for Arkansas (1700–1803) returned **1 total digitized volume** — the Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers (Image Group 008814402). This is the complete FamilySearch digitized set for Arkansas in this period. The Louisiana collections above are at the state/province level and are not limited to the Arkansas district.

### Physical Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Arkansas History Commission**, Little Rock, AR | Spanish colonial records, padrones, sacramental register transcriptions, land concession copies | In-person; some requests by mail/email |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | All Spanish colonial Louisiana records: administrative correspondence, military files, original land concessions, padrones, ecclesiastical records | In-person or via authorized researchers; partial digitization on PARES portal |
| **Library of Congress**, Washington, DC | Microfilm of selected Spanish colonial Louisiana records | In-person; some via interlibrary loan |
| **Roman Catholic Diocese of Little Rock** | Original or copies of Arkansas Post sacramental registers | Contact diocesan archives |
| **Newberry Library**, Chicago, IL | Strong holdings in colonial French and Spanish Mississippi Valley records | In-person; some digitized |
| **NARA Southwest Region**, Fort Worth, TX | Federal records post-1803 for Arkansas Territory | In-person / online catalog |

---

## Records NOT Online

The following are known to exist (per the FamilySearch Wiki's Arkansas Genealogy article, [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)) but were **not found in any digitized, name-indexed online collection**:

- **Padrones** (Spanish colonial household censuses) — Arkansas History Commission, Archivo General de Indias, Library of Congress microfilm
- **Spanish military garrison records** (muster rolls, officer correspondence) — Archivo General de Indias
- **Spanish land concession originals** — Archivo General de Indias
- **Pre-1763 French-era church registers** — Catholic Diocese of Little Rock and Arkansas History Commission; not in a digitized FamilySearch collection

---

## Known Record Losses

- **Arkansas Post was burned and rebuilt multiple times** during its colonial history; record survival is therefore fragmentary — do not assume a record never existed simply because it cannot be found
- The small scale of settlement (a single garrison post, never more than a few hundred European residents at any one time) means the total documentary output was modest compared to more populated colonial centers
- The administrative disruption of the Louisiana Purchase transition (1803) and the successive territorial reorganizations created gaps in record custody

---

## Research Tips

1. **Start with Image Group 008814402** (FamilySearch, free): browse all 64 images of the Arkansas Post Sacramental Registers, 1763–1800 — they are unindexed and in Spanish, but this is the only digitized primary source for the community's vital events during the Spanish period. ([FamilySearch Arkansas Genealogy — Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy#Colonial_Records))

2. **Search Louisiana before searching Arkansas**: Before 1819, "Arkansas" as a jurisdiction did not exist. FamilySearch's Louisiana Church Records (1612905, from 1718) and Louisiana Probate Records (2078341, from 1756) are both indexed and may capture individuals with Arkansas Post connections. Search Louisiana first.

3. **Use the AGI PARES portal** ([pares.cultura.gob.es](https://pares.cultura.gob.es)): Search under *Papeles de Cuba* for the Spanish colonial records of Louisiana. Arkansas Post commandant reports, land concessions, military records, and padrones are filed here. The portal has free digitized images of many documents.

4. **Land confirmation records are a high-yield substitute source**: Anyone holding Spanish-era land had to register their claim with the US Board of Land Commissioners after 1803. The sworn testimony names parents, settlement dates, neighbors, and witnesses — often providing more genealogical detail than any colonial record.

5. **Padrones are your census substitute**: When a family cannot be found in any church record, look for them in surviving Spanish padrones at the Arkansas History Commission or the AGI before concluding no record exists.

6. **Records are in French and/or Spanish**: Pre-1763 records are in French; 1763–1800 records are in Spanish. The Arkansas Post sacramental registers require a working knowledge of 18th-century Spanish ecclesiastical handwriting (*letra antigua*).

7. **FamilySearch wiki place pages for Arkansas** did not return Arkansas-specific content through the wiki tools — consult the [Arkansas Genealogy article](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy) directly and the Arkansas History Commission's own finding aids at its website.

8. **Search adjoining jurisdictions**: The neighboring French/Spanish colonial settlements in present-day Missouri (Ste. Geneviève, St. Louis) and Louisiana (Natchitoches, Natchez) generated records for some of the same population. Families near the Arkansas Post–Missouri border may appear in Upper Louisiana records filed under the predecessor Missouri Territory.

- Spanish garrison records at AGI (Papeles de Cuba); Library of Congress microfilm
- No digitized/indexed FamilySearch collection found

### Louisiana Church Records (Jurisdictional Overlap)
- FamilySearch Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 (collection 1612905; 987,654 records; indexed + images)
- Covers Louisiana jurisdiction from 1718 — may capture Arkansas district connections

## Repository Guide

### Online
| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | Image Group 008814402 (Arkansas Post registers 1763–1800); browse-only | Free |
| FamilySearch | Louisiana Church Records 1718–1925 (col. 1612905); indexed | Free |
| FamilySearch | Louisiana Probate Records 1756–1984 (col. 2078341); indexed | Free |
| AGI PARES | Papeles de Cuba — Spanish colonial Louisiana | Free |
| BLM GLO | Post-1803 land patents | Free |
| NARA | Land confirmations, military records | Free/in-person |

### Physical
| Repository | Holdings |
|---|---|
| Arkansas History Commission, Little Rock | Colonial records, padrones, register transcriptions |
| Archivo General de Indias, Seville | All Spanish colonial Louisiana records |
| Library of Congress | Microfilm of colonial Louisiana records |
| Catholic Diocese of Little Rock | Original sacramental registers |
| Newberry Library, Chicago | Colonial French/Spanish Mississippi Valley records |

## Records NOT Online
- Padrones (household censuses)
- Spanish military garrison records
- Spanish land concession originals
- Pre-1763 French-era church registers

## Known Losses
- Arkansas Post burned and rebuilt multiple times; record survival fragmentary
- Small settlement size limits total documentary output
- Administrative disruptions of 1803 transition created custody gaps

1. Browse FamilySearch Image Group 008814402 (64 images, Spanish, 1763–1800) — only digitized primary source for this community online
2. Search Louisiana collections first (before Arkansas) — FamilySearch Louisiana Church Records (1612905) and Probate Records (2078341) are indexed and cover the colonial period

5. Padrones at Arkansas History Commission and AGI are your census substitute
6. Records are in French (pre-1763) or Spanish (1763–1800) — must read original language
7. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Arkansas_Genealogy directly; FamilySearch wiki place pages returned only generic content through the tools

All tool results are in. Now I'll compile the complete guide from the tool data.

---

## 🗺️ Ohio Pre-Statehood Locality Guide
**Target Period:** c. 1787–1803 (Northwest Territory era through Ohio statehood)
**Canonical Place:** `Ohio, United States` (FamilySearch standard; date range from 1803)
**Research Focus:** Boundary changes, record availability, and substitute strategies for gaps

---

## Jurisdictional Context & Boundary Changes

**In 1790, present-day Ohio did not legally exist.** The land was organized as the **Northwest Territory**, created by the Northwest Ordinance of 1787. Ohio achieved statehood on March 1, 1803 — the first state carved from the Territory. Wikipedia confirms the Territory also encompassed what would become Indiana, Illinois, Michigan, Wisconsin, and part of Minnesota.

Within the Territory, only **two counties were organized** by 1790:

| County | Formed | Parent | Area Covered | Seat |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Washington County** | July 27, 1788 | Northwest Territory | Most of eastern & central Ohio | Marietta (first permanent American settlement) |
| **Hamilton County** | January 2, 1790 | Northwest Territory | Southwestern Ohio | Cincinnati |

All of **northern and northwestern Ohio remained unorganized territory** in 1790 — under direct territorial administration, with no county-level record-keeping infrastructure. Dozens of new counties were rapidly carved from Washington and Hamilton after 1800 as settlement expanded.

**The boundary-change rule here is temporal, not geographic:** When a new county was created from Washington or Hamilton County, records *before* that formation date stay under the parent county. You must trace the county-formation chain backward from your ancestor's known township to find the correct parent county and repository. The [FamilySearch Wiki (Ohio Genealogy — Northwest Territory section)](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Northwest_Territory) confirms: "Boundary changes were frequent — researchers must determine which county held jurisdiction at the time of the event. Early court and land records are held at the Ohio History Connection in Columbus."

### Three Distinct Land-Grant Systems — Different Repositories for Each

A geographic split overlaying the entire state means land records don't follow county boundaries alone. Each district has its own survey system and repository:

| District | Location in Ohio | Survey System | Key Repository |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Virginia Military District** | Between the Scioto and Little Miami rivers | Metes-and-bounds (irregular) | Virginia State Library, Richmond |
| **Connecticut Western Reserve** | Northeastern Ohio | Township grid (Connecticut survey) | Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland |
| **Federal survey lands** (Seven Ranges, Congress Lands, U.S. Military District, Symmes Purchase, etc.) | Remainder of Ohio | Rectangular (township-range) | BLM General Land Office ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) |

*(Source: [Ohio Genealogy — FamilySearch Wiki, Land Records section](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Genealogy#Land_Records)).*

**Identify which district your ancestor's land fell in before searching** — the wrong district search will find nothing even when records survive.

---

## Record-by-Record Survey

### 🌟 Land Records — Best Source for 1790 Ohio

Land is the richest record class for this period. Settlers acquired land before almost any other government record was created.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Ohio, Land Records, 1787–1840"** (Collection 1542187) — 234,567 records, 117,283 images. Starts 1787, directly covering the territorial era. Name-indexed and searchable. → [familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542187)

**FamilySearch digitized volume (⚠️ browse-only):**
- Image group **005112233** — "Northwest Territory, Territorial Land Records, 1788–1799" — 51 images. **0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable. Must be browsed image-by-image.** Note that this volume is catalogued under **"Northwest Territory, United States"**, not "Ohio" — FamilySearch models the pre-1803 period separately.

**Off-FamilySearch repositories (required for full coverage):**
- Virginia Military District warrants → Virginia State Library
- Connecticut Western Reserve → Western Reserve Historical Society, Cleveland
- Federal land patents → BLM GLO website (searchable online free)
- Deed books and court land records → Ohio History Connection, Columbus; county courthouses (Washington Co. at Marietta; Hamilton Co. at Cincinnati)

---

### 📋 Tax Records — Best Annual Substitute for Missing Census

Tax lists name heads of household every year and are the primary bridge back to 1790 when census coverage failed.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Ohio, Tax Records, 1800–1850"** (Collection 1987542) — 345,890 records, 172,945 images. Begins 1800 — just after our target window but captures the statehood transition. → [familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987542)

**FamilySearch digitized volume (⚠️ mostly browse-only):**
- Image group **005112240** — "Washington County, Ohio, County Tax Records, 1799–1803" — 73 images. **Only 12% name-indexed; not full-text searchable.** The remaining 88% must be browsed manually.

*Gap:* Pre-1799 territorial tax records are **not represented in FamilySearch's indexed or digitized collections** based on the volume search (totalResults: 2). Physical or microfilm records from this period may survive at the Ohio History Connection or Washington/Hamilton county archives — check there directly.

---

### 💒 Church Records — Critical Vital Substitute

With no civil vital registration in 1790, church registers are the **only systematic source** for births (as baptisms), marriages, and deaths (as burials) in the earliest Ohio settlements.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Ohio, Church Records, 1787–1950"** (Collection 2246917) — 678,234 records, 339,117 images. Starts 1787, overlapping the first year of American settlement. → [familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2246917)

**Key early denominations:** Presbyterian, Methodist Episcopal, Baptist, Quaker (Friends), German Reformed, Lutheran. Additional records may be held at denominational archives and local churches not yet digitized.

---

### 💍 Marriage Records

Unlike births and deaths, **county-level marriage recording began with county formation** — making marriage records the exception to the vital records gap.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **"Ohio, County Marriages, 1789–2013"** (Collection 1803785) — 1,523,678 records, 761,839 images. Starts **1789** (Washington County's first full year). → [familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1803785)

This is a major indexed resource for the period. Hamilton County marriages begin from 1790.

---

### 🏛️ Vital Records (Births & Deaths) — ⚠️ Major Gap

**No civil registration of births or deaths existed in Ohio in 1790.** Ohio statehood came in 1803, and even then statewide civil vital registration came much later. The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Ohio Vital Records returned only generic (non-Ohio-specific) content from tool queries — no Ohio-specific registration start date can be confirmed from the tool results. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [Ohio Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Vital_Records) for confirmed dates.

*Substitutes:* Church baptism/burial registers (see Church Records above), probate estate inventories, and family Bible records.

---

### 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦 Census Records

- **1790 Federal Census:** Ohio was enumerated as part of the Northwest Territory. However, coverage was **extremely incomplete and much of the Ohio portion is lost or was never taken** for this sparsely settled frontier. Non-appearance does not mean an ancestor wasn't there.
- **1800 Federal Census** is the first reasonably complete enumeration for Ohio and is the practical earliest starting point.
- No territorial or state census existed for Ohio in 1790.
- Access via: NARA ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov)) and Ancestry.com ([ancestry.com/search/collections/census](https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/))

---

### ⚖️ Probate Records

Probate (wills, estate inventories, guardianships, administrations) began with county court formation:
- **Washington County**: from 1788 (Marietta seat)
- **Hamilton County**: from 1790 (Cincinnati seat)

The FamilySearch Wiki page for Ohio Probate Records returned only generic content — specific digitized collections cannot be confirmed from tool results. Physical records are held at county courthouses and the Ohio History Connection. Consult [Ohio Probate Records — FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Ohio_Probate_Records) directly.

---

### 🪖 Military Records

- **Revolutionary War service, pensions, and bounty land warrants:** NARA and Fold3 ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)). Many early Ohio settlers were veterans claiming land bounties — **bounty land warrant records at NARA and BLM GLO often predate any other Ohio record for an individual.**
- The Virginia Military District was *specifically* set aside for Virginia's veterans — check Virginia records even for ancestors who later settled in Ohio.
- Territorial militia records may be at the Ohio History Connection.

---

### 📰 Newspapers & Cemetery Records

- **Newspapers:** The first Ohio newspaper (*The Centinel of the North-Western Territory*) began in Cincinnati in 1793. Very limited digitized coverage exists for 1790. → Newspapers.com ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/))
- **Cemetery / Burial Records:** Find A Grave ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)). Few 1790-era gravestones survive in readable condition; many early settlers had unmarked frontier graves.

---

## Digitization Coverage Summary

| Record Type | Collection / Volume | Period | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|
| Land Records | Collection 1542187 | 1787–1840 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Land Records (territorial) | Vol. 005112233 | 1788–1799 | 🔍 Browse-only (0% indexed) |
| Marriage Records | Collection 1803785 | 1789–2013 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Church Records | Collection 2246917 | 1787–1950 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Tax Records | Collection 1987542 | 1800–1850 | ✅ Indexed + images |
| Tax Records (Washington Co.) | Vol. 005112240 | 1799–1803 | ⚠️ 12% indexed, 88% browse-only |
| Birth / Death Records | — | 1790 | ❌ No civil registration — use church records |
| Census (1790) | NARA / Ancestry | 1790 | ⚠️ Largely lost / fragmentary |
| Probate Records | County courthouses / OHC | From 1788 | 🏛️ Mostly physical — not confirmed digitized |
| Pre-1799 Tax Records | — | 1788–1799 | 🏛️ Physical only (OHC / county archives) |

*(Volume search totalResults: 2 for 1780–1810 window; both detailed above. Collections search: 5 total for Ohio, 4 of 5 overlap the target period.)*

---

## Key Quirks for Pre-Statehood Ohio Research

1. **Jurisdiction first — always.** "Ohio" didn't exist in 1790. Every record was created under the Northwest Territory and filed under either **Washington County** (eastern/central Ohio) or **Hamilton County** (southwestern Ohio), or not at all (unorganized northern Ohio). Establish which county held authority *at the time of the event*.

2. **FamilySearch indexes Ohio from 1803; territorial volumes appear under "Northwest Territory, United States."** Search both labels when browsing volumes.

3. **Three land systems, three repositories.** Identify your ancestor's land district (Virginia Military District / Connecticut Western Reserve / federal survey) before searching — the wrong district search will miss existing records entirely.

4. **The 1790 Ohio census is largely lost.** Begin with 1800 as your earliest reliable census. Bridge back to 1790 with tax lists and land records.

5. **No civil birth or death registration existed in 1790.** Church baptism and burial registers are the only systematic vital substitute. Absence from church records may mean an event is effectively undocumentable.

6. **Bounty land warrants often predate Ohio settlement.** Veterans could claim their Virginia Military District or U.S. Military District land before emigrating — check NARA and Virginia records even for ancestors not yet in Ohio.

7. **Records before 1803 may sit under the predecessor jurisdiction's county, not any county the place belongs to today.** Always trace the county-formation chain backward.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **Ohio History Connection**, Columbus | Territorial & early-state court, land, and government records | On-site; some digitized |
| **NARA** (National Archives) | Federal census, military, pension, naturalization | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov) |
| **BLM General Land Office** | Federal land patents (rectangular-survey lands) | [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) (free online) |
| **Virginia State Library**, Richmond | Virginia Military District warrants | On-site; some digitized |
| **Western Reserve Historical Society**, Cleveland | Connecticut Western Reserve records | On-site |
| **Washington County courthouse**, Marietta | Earliest county records (from 1788) | On-site |
