output.text_response:
I'll survey California's 1850s Gold Rush records for you. Let me start by establishing the jurisdictional context.

Good — California became a state in 1850, so the Gold Rush decade (1848–1860) spans both pre-statehood (military government, 1848–1850) and early statehood. Now I'll run the full parallel survey.

Now I have enough to compile the full guide. Here is the California Gold Rush locality survey:

---

## 📍 California, United States — Locality Research Guide
### Target Period: 1848–1865 (Gold Rush Era)

---

### Jurisdictional Context

Gold was discovered at Sutter's Mill on **January 24, 1848**, while California was still under U.S. military government following the Mexican-American War. California **bypassed territorial status entirely** and was admitted as a state on **September 9, 1850** — meaning records from 1848–1850 predate any formal civilian county infrastructure. By the early 1850s, 27 original counties had been created, and county recorders became the primary record-keepers for vital events, land, and court matters. The Gold Rush brought an estimated **300,000 migrants** from across the United States and abroad (Wikipedia).

> **⚠️ Quirk:** California had no territorial period. There is no territorial-era civil record system — the pre-statehood years (1848–1850) rely almost entirely on military registers, ship manifests, church records, and private documentation.

---

### Digitization Overview (FamilySearch Collections)

FamilySearch's `collections_search` returned **4 indexed collections** covering this period for California:

| Collection | Date Range | Records | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| [California, County Births, 1850–1919](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) | 1850–1919 | 789,456 | **Indexed + images** |
| [California, County Marriages, 1850–1952](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) | 1850–1952 | 567,890 persons | **Indexed + images** |
| [California, Great Registers, 1866–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) | 1866–1910 | 1,345,678 | **Indexed + images** |
| [California, Mission Records, 1769–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) | 1769–1850 | 98,765 | **Indexed + images** |

`volume_search` found **14 digitized volumes** in total for 1848–1865; the first page details three:

| Volume | Place | Dates | Images | Access Level |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 006601001 | California (statewide) | 1850–1852 | 522 | **Indexed + full-text** (88% name-indexed) |
| 006601002 | San Francisco | 1849–1855 | 340 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) |
| 006601003 | Sacramento | 1849–1858 | 298 | ⚠️ **Browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable) |

> **Note:** 14 total digitized volumes match this search; only the first 3 are detailed above. Additional volumes may be retrieved by requesting the next page.

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

---

#### 1. 🗳️ Census Records — **START HERE**

**1852 California State Census** *(Volume 006601001)*
This is the single most powerful starting point for Gold Rush research. It is 88% name-indexed and fully full-text searchable on FamilySearch. With 522 images covering the whole state, it was taken just two years after the first rush and captures the transient mining population at its peak. Search it at FamilySearch before any other record type.

**1850 U.S. Federal Census** *(first federal census for California)*
> ⚠️ **Critical gap:** The 1850 federal census for California was **partially destroyed** — some county returns are missing entirely. Do not assume absence from the 1850 census means your ancestor wasn't there; consult the 1852 state census as the primary substitute. ([FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, Pre-Statehood Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Pre-Statehood_Records))

**1860 U.S. Federal Census** captures those who remained after the main rush subsided and is intact for California.

---

#### 2. ⛏️ Mining Claim Records — **Gold Rush-Specific**

**Mining Claim Registers, San Francisco area, 1849–1855** *(Volume 006601002)*
> ⚠️ **Browse-only.** 340 images, 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable. Must be browsed image-by-image with no search capability. These registers recorded individual miners' claims to specific placer or lode deposits.

County recorders' offices also hold mining claim records. The FamilySearch Wiki notes these are at county recorders' offices for each Gold Rush county (El Dorado, Placer, Nevada, Tuolumne, Calaveras, Amador, etc.). ([FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

---

#### 3. ⛵ Ship Passenger Manifests & Arrival Records

**Port Arrival Registers, Sacramento, 1849–1858** *(Volume 006601003)*
> ⚠️ **Browse-only.** 298 images, 0% name-indexed, NOT full-text searchable. Browse image-by-image.

**San Francisco ship passenger manifests** are held at the **National Archives, Pacific Region (San Bruno, California)** — the primary repository for arrivals around Cape Horn or via Panama. The FamilySearch Wiki specifically identifies these as a key source for migrants who came by sea. ([FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy, Gold Rush Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy#Gold_Rush_Records))

Overland arrivals are documented through **trail diaries, journals, and emigrant guides** held at the California State Library and the Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley.

---

#### 4. 📜 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

California had **no statewide civil registration** during the Gold Rush decade. Registration was at the **county level**, beginning with statehood in 1850.

- **Births:** [California, County Births, 1850–1919](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2017276) — indexed + images on FamilySearch (789,456 records). Coverage is uneven in the early 1850s because county infrastructure was just being established.
- **Marriages:** [California, County Marriages, 1850–1952](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1452832) — indexed + images on FamilySearch (567,890 persons).
- **Deaths:** No county death collection for this period was returned by FamilySearch's `collections_search`. Death records for the 1850s are a **coverage gap** — check church burial registers, cemetery records (Find A Grave), and newspaper obituaries as substitutes.

> **⚠️ Vital Records wiki page note:** The specific California Vital Records FamilySearch Wiki page was not returned by the tool — it redirected to generic content. Do not rely on assumed statewide registration dates; county-level collection coverage (from 1850) is the verified starting point for this period.

---

#### 5. 🗳️ Voter Registration — Great Registers

[California, Great Registers, 1866–1910](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1923340) — **1,345,678 records, indexed + images.**

These begin in **1866**, after the main rush, but they are exceptional sources for men who settled in California after migrating for gold. Each entry typically records the voter's name, age, birthplace, occupation, physical description, and county of residence — a rich biographical snapshot. Even if your ancestor arrived in 1849, his 1866 or later Great Register entry will confirm he stayed and give you details to verify identity.

---

#### 6. ⛪ Church Records

Mission Records (Spanish/Mexican era, pre-Gold Rush background context):
- [California, Mission Records, 1769–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1804372) — 98,765 records, indexed + images. These cover the Catholic Mission system and are primarily relevant for Hispanic California families or Native California ancestry, not for 49er migrants. The series ends at 1850.

For Gold Rush-era Protestant and Catholic churches in the mining counties, records are held at **denominational archives** and the **California State Library**. FamilySearch microfilm holdings vary by county and congregation.

---

#### 7. 🏡 Land Records

California is a **federal land state** — original land patents were issued by the Bureau of Land Management (BLM). Search free at:
- **[BLM General Land Office Records](https://glorecords.blm.gov/)** — patents, surveys, and land entry case files for federal lands

Pre-existing Mexican land grants (ranchos) were subject to confirmation proceedings before the U.S. Land Commission (1851–1856). These records are at the **National Archives, San Bruno**, and at the **Bancroft Library**.

County deed books (post-1850) are at county recorders' offices. FamilySearch `volume_search` did not return specifically identified land deed volumes for 1848–1865 in the first-page results; check FamilySearch catalog by county for microfilmed deed series.

---

#### 8. 🏛️ Probate & Court Records

- **Probate records** (wills, estate inventories, guardianships) are at county superior courts and county archives. Many 49ers died intestate; intestacy proceedings can still document heirs and kin.
- **Naturalization records** (pre-1906) were filed in any court of record — county, district, or federal. The large foreign-born mining population (Irish, Chinese, German, Chilean, Mexican, French) makes these especially productive. NARA San Bruno holds federal-court naturalizations; county courthouses hold state-court filings.

---

#### 9. ✉️ Military Records

Veterans of the Mexican-American War (1846–1848) who stayed in California as 49ers may have pension files at NARA. Civil War service records (1861–1865) are on **[Fold3](https://www.fold3.com/)** and at NARA, Washington, D.C. The California State Archives holds state adjutant general records.

---

#### 10. 📰 Newspapers

California had a vigorous Gold Rush–era newspaper press. Mining-town papers published notices of arrivals, deaths, property transfers, and court proceedings.
- **[Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)** — subscription, broad California coverage
- **California Digital Newspaper Collection** (UC Riverside) — free, concentrates on 19th-century papers
- **California State Library** newspaper microfilm holdings (Sacramento)

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch.org** | Census (1852), births, marriages, mission records, Great Registers, some mining/arrival volumes | Free online |
| **NARA Pacific Region, San Bruno, CA** | Ship passenger manifests, federal court naturalizations, Mexican land grant proceedings | In-person or records requests |
| **California State Archives (Sacramento)** | State-level records, adjutant general, legislative records | In-person |
| **California State Library (Sacramento)** | Manuscript collections, newspapers, Gold Rush diaries | In-person |
| **Bancroft Library, UC Berkeley** | Gold Rush manuscripts, overland emigrant journals, rancho records | In-person (UC affiliation or visiting researcher) |
| **County Recorders' Offices** | Mining claim registers, deeds, early vital records | County-level; some digitized |
| **BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov)** | Federal land patents | Free online |
| **Find A Grave (findagrave.com)** | Cemetery records, memorial photos | Free online |
| **Fold3 (fold3.com)** | Military service records, pension files | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Subscription |

---

### Research Strategy Notes

1. **Start with the 1852 California State Census** — it is highly indexed, full-text searchable, and taken at the height of the rush. Cross it against the 1860 federal census to track who stayed.
2. **The 1850 federal census has county-level gaps** from destruction — never treat a 49er's absence there as proof they weren't in California.
3. **Mining claim registers are browse-only.** Plan time to scroll through images by county if you need them.
4. **Ship manifests at NARA San Bruno** are the entry point for sea migrants; Bancroft Library diaries and journals serve overland arrivals.
5. **Great Registers (from 1866)** are the best "where did he end up?" source for men who survived the rush — rich biographical detail, name-indexed, and free on FamilySearch.
6. **Death records are a gap** for the 1850s. Use church burial registers, newspaper notices, probate records, and Find A Grave as substitutes.
7. **For foreign-born miners** (Chinese, Irish, German, Chilean, etc.), naturalization records and the Great Registers are critical — the Great Registers note birthplace and physical description.
8. **The FamilySearch wiki_place_page** for California returned only generic content in all four sections (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) rather than California-specific guidance. Consult [FamilySearch Wiki — California Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/California_Genealogy) directly for the most current collection links and research tips.

---

This is a standalone survey (no active research project detected), so no persistence step is needed. If you'd like a targeted research plan for a specific ancestor or county, just let me know — I can focus the next step on exactly where they were mining or settling.

Now I have enough to compile the guide. Here is what I found from the tools, annotated by reliability:

---

## 🗽 Locality Research Guide: New York City, 1700s (Colonial Period)

### Jurisdictional Context

During the 1700s, what we call "New York City" was legally the City of New York, occupying the lower end of Manhattan Island — roughly coextensive with **New York County**. The surrounding counties were separate jurisdictions that today form the outer boroughs:

| County (1700s name) | Today's Borough | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **New York County** | Manhattan | The city proper; where most colonial records originate |
| **Kings County** | Brooklyn | Separate jurisdiction; Dutch-settled, distinct records |
| **Queens County** | Queens | Separate jurisdiction |
| **Richmond County** | Staten Island | Separate jurisdiction |
| **Westchester County** | Parts of the Bronx | The Bronx area was Westchester County through much of this period |

The city was under **British colonial rule** throughout the 1700s (Province of New York), following the Dutch colonial period (1626–1664). Many record series continued in Dutch language well into the British period, particularly in church registers. New York served as the provincial capital and a major Atlantic commercial port.

**Cross-border note:** Families near the Hudson River may have also generated records in **New Jersey** (East and West Jersey, later the royal colony of New Jersey). Always check New Jersey county records — Bergen and Essex Counties especially — for families with NYC connections.

> ⚠️ **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York State** (all four sections: home, getting started, online records, research tips) and specific pages for New York Vital Records, Church Records, Land Records, and Probate Records **all returned only generic content** from these tool calls — not New York-specific guidance. Claims below are grounded strictly in `collections_search`, `volume_search`, and `wiki_search` results. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy) for the full state-level guide.

---

### Vital Records

**There was no civil registration of births, marriages, or deaths in colonial New York.** No statewide or city-level civil vital registration system existed in the 1700s. **Church records are the essential substitute** for the entire colonial period — if your ancestor was not connected to a congregation, direct vital evidence may not survive.

---

### 1. Church Records ⭐ Prime Source

Church registers — baptisms, marriages, and burials — are the colonial-era equivalent of vital records.

**Key denominations in 1700s NYC** (from `wiki_search`):
- **Dutch Reformed Church** — oldest continuous series, beginning 1639. Registers run through the entire colonial period and beyond. ⚠️ Records are in **Dutch**; the researcher must read the original language.
- **Anglican — Trinity Church** — the established Church of England congregation; records cover baptisms, marriages, and burials for the city's English population.
- **Presbyterian** — growing congregation by mid-century; records survive.
- Additional congregations: Lutheran, Quaker, Jewish (Shearith Israel, the oldest congregation in North America, has records from this period), French Huguenot.

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- **New York, Church Records, 1640–1940** (Collection ID: [1469062](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1469062)) — **~2.3 million records / ~1.17 million images** — indexed and browsable on FamilySearch.

**Digitized volume found via `volume_search`:**
- **Image Group 007733180** — Dutch Reformed Church Registers, New York City, **1700–1776** — 211 images — **⚠️ Browse-only: 0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable, in Dutch.** Must be paged through image by image; requires Dutch-language reading ability.

**Other repositories:**
- **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society (NYGBS)** — holds transcriptions and indexes of many NYC church registers; their *New York Genealogical and Biographical Record* journal published many colonial church abstracts.
- **New-York Historical Society (NYHS)** — holds original and microfilmed registers.
- Individual denomination archives (e.g., Episcopal Diocese of New York for Trinity Church records).

---

### 2. Land Records ⭐ Prime Source

Land records are among the most consistently surviving colonial-era sources and often name family members, neighbors, and witnesses.

Types useful for the 1700s:
- **Land patents and grants** — issued by the colonial governor; New York Colonial Manuscripts at the New York State Archives.
- **Deeds and conveyances** — recorded at the county level (New York County Deed Books).
- **Quit-rent lists** — periodic lists of landholders paying annual rent to the Crown.

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- **New York, Land Records, 1630–1975** (Collection ID: [2078654](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078654)) — **~1.57 million records / ~784,000 images** — indexed and browsable.

**Repository:** New York County Clerk's Office holds original deed books; New York State Archives holds colonial-era grants and patents.

---

### 3. Probate Records ⭐ Prime Source

Wills and estate records are rich sources — they name heirs, identify relationships, and describe property.

**Colonial probate jurisdiction:** Wills in colonial New York were proved before the **Prerogative Court of New York** (a provincial court), not at the county level. The **New-York Historical Society** published the *Abstracts of Wills* series, which indexes wills proved in colonial New York — this is a key finding aid for the 1700s. (Source: `wiki_search` result from [New York City Genealogy — Tax and Military Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_City_Genealogy#Tax_and_Military_Records))

**FamilySearch Collection:**
- **New York, Probate Records, 1629–1971** (Collection ID: [1542780](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1542780)) — **~988,000 records / ~494,000 images** — indexed and browsable.

**Repository:** New York State Archives holds original Prerogative Court records; NYHS holds the published *Abstracts of Wills*.

---

### 4. Court Records

- **Mayor's Court of New York City** — the primary civil court for the colonial city; records name parties, witnesses, and often relationships. (Source: `wiki_search`)
- **New York Colonial Manuscripts** — held at the **New York State Archives**, Albany; cover the full colonial period including court proceedings, council minutes, and administrative records.
- Court records may also include early naturalization proceedings.

---

### 5. Tax and Military Records

- **Colonial tax assessment lists** — ward-level lists survive for some years and can identify residents and their relative wealth. (Source: `wiki_search`)
- **Colonial militia rolls** — list men of military age; useful for identifying adult male residents by neighborhood/ward. (Source: `wiki_search`)
- **FamilySearch Collection (borderline):** *New York, Tax Assessment Rolls of Real and Personal Estates, 1799–1804* (Collection ID: [1678432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678432)) — **~123,000 records** — this starts at the very end of the colonial period and into the early republic, but is the earliest tax collection digitized on FamilySearch.

---

### 6. Census & Population Lists

- **No federal census** existed before 1790. The first federal census (1790) catches families just after the colonial period ends.
- **Provincial censuses and militia musters** were taken periodically by the colonial government — these are in the New York Colonial Manuscripts at the State Archives, not on FamilySearch.
- The **1790 U.S. Federal Census** (available on FamilySearch and Ancestry) is the first broad population listing and may help confirm families present at the close of the colonial period.

---

### 7. Newspapers

- The **New-York Gazette** (founded 1725) and other colonial newspapers published vital notices (marriages, deaths), runaway notices, and other family-relevant items.
- **Newspapers.com** and **Readex's America's Historical Newspapers** hold digitized colonial-era NYC newspapers. (External links search returned Newspapers.com as a curated resource.)

---

### 8. Military Records (Revolutionary War transition)

For families spanning the late colonial period into the Revolution (1775–1783):
- **Fold3** holds Revolutionary War service and pension records at NARA. (External links search returned Fold3 as a curated resource.)
- **NARA** (National Archives) holds compiled military service records for Continental Army soldiers and loyalist claims records.

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Church records, land, probate, tax (see collections above) | Free online |
| **New York State Archives** (Albany) | Colonial Manuscripts, provincial court records, governor's papers | Physical & some online |
| **New York Genealogical & Biographical Society** (nygbs.org) | Church abstracts, NYGBR journal, colonial indexes | Membership/subscription |
| **New-York Historical Society** (nyhistory.org) | *Abstracts of Wills*, church registers, manuscript collections | On-site & some digital |
| **New York City Municipal Archives** | City government records (some dating to the colonial period) | On-site & some online |
| **NARA — Northeast Region** (New York City) | Federal records, Revolutionary War files | On-site |

---

### Research Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Dutch-language records** persist well into the British period — Dutch Reformed Church registers through the 1700s are in Dutch. Budget for translation or use published transcriptions.
2. **Pre-1664 records** from the Dutch period (New Amsterdam) are in Dutch and held partly in the Netherlands; for 1700s research this is background context, not a prime source.
3. **Probate was provincial, not county-level** in colonial NY — search the Prerogative Court records and NYHS *Abstracts of Wills*, not just county probate files.
4. **No civil vital registration** existed until the 19th century — church affiliation is essential. If an ancestor belonged to no known congregation, surviving evidence is thin.
5. **The outer boroughs were separate counties** in the 1700s — Kings, Queens, and Richmond County each kept their own records; do not assume Manhattan/New York County records cover all of what is now "NYC."
6. **1790 Federal Census** is the earliest broad population snapshot; work backward from it using church, land, and probate records for the pre-1790 decades.
7. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for New York** returned only generic content in this survey — consult the wiki directly for updates: [familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Genealogy).

---

### Digitization Summary

| Record Type | FamilySearch Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Church Records | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 1469062) | 1 browse-only Dutch Reformed vol. (007733180, Dutch, 1700–1776) |
| Land Records | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 2078654) | |
| Probate Records | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 1542780) | |
| Tax Records | ✅ Indexed + images (Collection 1678432) | Starts 1799 only |
| Colonial Manuscripts / Court | ⚠️ Physical only | New York State Archives, Albany |
| Militia / Provincial Census | ⚠️ Physical only | New York State Archives |
| Newspapers | ✅ External sites | Newspapers.com, Readex |

Here is the locality research guide for Virginia, 1775–1783, compiled from the tool results.

---

# Virginia, 1775–1783 — Revolutionary War Research Guide

## Jurisdictional Context

Virginia was one of the original Thirteen Colonies and maintained **county-level record-keeping from the 1630s**, making it one of the best-documented colonial jurisdictions in America. According to Wikipedia, Virginia contributed more troops to the Continental Army than any other colony; major engagements including the decisive siege at Yorktown (1781) were fought on Virginia soil. The state functioned as a commonwealth throughout the war and was formally admitted under its current status in 1788.

> ⚠️ **Critical gap:** The **1790 federal census for Virginia is entirely lost** — destroyed when the British burned Washington in 1814. The FamilySearch Wiki confirms that **1780s county personal property tax lists** are the principal population-wide substitute. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

> ℹ️ **Wiki coverage note:** All four `wiki_place_page` sections (home / getting_started / online_records / research_tips) and four constructed Virginia wiki URLs (Virginia_Vital_Records, Virginia_Military_Records, Virginia_Land_and_Property, Virginia_Genealogy) returned only generic content in this session. Virginia-specific details below come from the `wiki_search` results; visit [familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records) directly for the full article.

---

## 1. Military Service Records — The Primary Track

### A. Continental Army Service Records & Muster Rolls — NARA Record Group 93
Per the FamilySearch Wiki ([Virginia Military Records — Revolutionary War](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Revolutionary_War)):
- Service records and muster rolls for **Virginia Continental Line** soldiers
- Held at the **National Archives and Records Administration (NARA)** | [archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)
- Also digitized and searchable via **Fold3** (see §6 below)

### B. Virginia Militia Records — Library of Virginia
- Per the FamilySearch Wiki, **Virginia militia records** are held at the **Library of Virginia**, Richmond | [lva.virginia.gov](https://lva.virginia.gov/)
- Militia service is a **separate record series** from Continental records — a man may appear in one but not the other; both must be searched independently

### C. FamilySearch Collection: Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783
- **Collection:** [Virginia, Military Records, 1775–1783](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1945678) (ID: 1945678)
- Date range exactly matches the war years
- **Access:** Free at FamilySearch

### D. Virginia State Navy Records
- The FamilySearch Wiki identifies published **Virginia State Navy records** as a distinct key source for maritime wartime service

---

## 2. Pension Files & Bounty-Land Warrants — Post-War Documentation of Service

### A. Pension & Bounty-Land Warrant Applications — NARA Record Group 15
- Application files for Revolutionary War **pensions and bounty-land warrants**
- Genealogically rich: files often contain the veteran's deposition, affidavits from neighbors and family, and widow's applications with marriage and death information
- Held at NARA; also available via **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) — flagged by FamilySearch as a curated external resource for this time window

### B. Revolutionary War Land Bounty Warrants — Digitized Volume (Browse-Only)
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Image Group | 005301447 |
| Images | 341 |
| Coverage | Virginia, 1779–1800 |
| Indexed? | ⚠️ **0% name-indexed** |
| Full-text searchable? | ❌ No |
| **Access level** | **Browse-only — images must be viewed one by one; no search** |

After the war, Virginia granted bounty lands in the **Virginia Military District of Ohio** to its veterans. Warrant and survey records at the **Virginia State Library** connect veterans to their land claims. ([Virginia Military Records — Post-War Bounty Lands](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Military_Records#Post-War_Bounty_Lands))

---

## 3. Tax Records — The 1790 Census Substitute

Because the 1790 Virginia census was destroyed, **personal property tax lists from 1782–1785** are the primary population-wide substitute. They list taxable white males over 21 along with taxable property, making them essential for locating households during and immediately after the war.

### A. State Enumerations / Tax Lists — Digitized Volume (Full-Text Searchable)
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Image Group | 005301449 |
| Images | 87 |
| Coverage | Virginia, 1782–1799 |
| Indexed? | 0% name-indexed |
| Full-text searchable? | ✅ **Yes** — searchable by text via FamilySearch fulltext search |
| **Access level** | **Full-text searchable; not name-indexed** |

### B. FamilySearch Collection: Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850
- **Collection:** [Virginia, Tax Records, 1782–1850](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1456723) (ID: 1456723)
- Begins at the close of the war — covers the critical post-war decade

---

## 4. Land & Property Records

### FamilySearch Collection: Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900
- **Collection:** [Virginia, Land, Marriage, and Will Records, 1600–1900](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1734285) (ID: 1734285)
- Virginia is a **state-land state** — land grants derive from the colonial/state government, not the federal government; deed books and grants are held at county courthouses and the Library of Virginia
- Wartime land transactions (sales, grants, estate divisions) can document family relationships and residence

---

## 5. County Court Records

### A. FamilySearch Collection: Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920
- **Collection:** [Virginia, County Court Records, 1650–1920](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134567) (ID: 2134567)
- County courts handled estate settlements, road orders, militia officer appointments, and civil suits — all potential wartime documentation

### B. Augusta County Court Order Books, 1775–1795 — Digitized Volume (Partially Indexed)
| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| Image Group | 005301448 |
| Images | 158 |
| Coverage | Augusta County, Virginia, 1775–1795 |
| Indexed? | ✅ **61% name-indexed** |
| Full-text searchable? | No |
| **Access level** | **Partially indexed + images** — most records reachable by name search; remainder browse-only |

Augusta County in the Shenandoah Valley was a major source of frontier militia. Its court order books are among the better-indexed volumes for this period.

---

## 6. Church Records

### FamilySearch Collection: Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929
- **Collection:** [Virginia, Church Records, 1680–1929](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598230) (ID: 1598230)
- In 1775–1783, Virginia had **no civil vital registration** — the Anglican (Episcopal) Church was the established church; its vestry books recorded baptisms, marriages, and burials. Dissenting denominations (Baptist, Presbyterian, Methodist) kept separate registers.
- These are the **primary source for vital events** during the war years

---

## 7. Newspapers

**Newspapers.com** | [newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/) *(subscription)*
- Virginia newspapers from the 1770s–1780s (notably the *Virginia Gazette*, Williamsburg) published:
  - Military appointment and promotion lists
  - Deserter notices
  - Pension and land-bounty advertisements
  - Loyalist proceedings and property confiscation notices

---

## 8. Cemetery Records

**Find A Grave** | [findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/) *(free)*
- Memorial entries often document Revolutionary War service via DAR/SAR grave markers, veteran rolls, and published pension lists

---

## Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **NARA** ([archives.gov](https://www.archives.gov/)) | Continental service records (RG 93); pension & bounty-land files (RG 15) | Free in-person; via Fold3 online |
| **Library of Virginia** ([lva.virginia.gov](https://lva.virginia.gov/)) | Virginia militia records; state military & legislative records | Free online catalog; some digitized |
| **FamilySearch** ([familysearch.org](https://www.familysearch.org/)) | 5 collections + 3 digitized volumes covering 1775–1783 | Free |
| **Fold3** ([fold3.com](https://www.fold3.com/)) | Digitized RevWar pension files, service records, muster rolls | Subscription |
| **Ancestry** ([ancestry.com](https://www.ancestry.com/)) | U.S. census and Virginia record collections | Subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** ([newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com/)) | Virginia newspapers, 1770s–1780s | Subscription |
| **Find A Grave** ([findagrave.com](https://www.findagrave.com/)) | Cemetery memorials, veteran markers | Free |

---

## Key Quirks & Cautions

1. **Missing 1790 Virginia Census.** Use the 1782–1785 personal property tax lists as the primary population substitute — the FamilySearch full-text-searchable volume (IGN 005301449) covers 1782–1799.
2. **Two parallel military tracks.** Continental Army records (NARA RG 93) and Virginia militia records (Library of Virginia) are separate series. Always search both — a man who appears in neither may still show up in pension files.
3. **Bounty-land records bridge service gaps.** Post-war warrant and survey records document service even when wartime muster rolls are missing or destroyed.
4. **No civil vital registration in 1775–1783.** Church vestry books (Anglican/Episcopal) and dissenting congregation registers are the only vital-event sources for this period. The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Virginia-specific registration start dates in this session — consult [Virginia Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Virginia_Vital_Records) directly.
5. **Bounty-land warrants (IGN 005301447) are browse-only.** With 341 images, 0% indexed, and no full-text search, this volume requires image-by-image browsing — plan accordingly.
6. **Fold3 is the leading online access point** for digitized pension files and service records and should be used alongside the free NARA catalog.

---

This guide covers the main avenues for Virginia Revolutionary War research. If you'd like to narrow to a specific county, military district, or record type — or proceed to a research plan or record searches — just say the word.

# 🗺️ Locality Research Guide
## New Orleans (Orleans Parish), Louisiana — Early 1800s (c. 1800–1850)

---

## Jurisdictional Context

New Orleans sits in **Orleans Parish**, one of Louisiana's original parishes established in 1807. The early 1800s span four successive sovereigns, which directly determines what record systems existed and which survive:

| Period | Sovereign / Status | Record System |
|---|---|---|
| ~1800 | Spain cedes to France (Treaty of San Ildefonso) | Spanish civil law & Catholic registers |
| 1800–1803 | French (brief) | Catholic registers; few new civil records |
| 1803–1812 | **Territory of Orleans** (U.S.) | Transition to American administration; Spanish/French-era record series continued |
| From Apr. 30, 1812 | **State of Louisiana** | State civil law system begins; U.S. land office, federal census |

Louisiana retained the **civil law tradition** (derived from the Napoleonic Code, not English common law). This means researchers encounter uniquely Louisiana record types throughout the early 1800s: **successions** (the Louisiana equivalent of probate), **tutorships** (guardianship of minors), and **interdictions** (civil incapacity proceedings). These are not called wills or probate — terminology matters when searching.

The FamilySearch `standardPlace` is **"New Orleans, Orleans, Louisiana, United States"** (city founded 1718). The state `standardPlace` is **"Louisiana, United States"** (statehood from 1812).

---

## Disasters That Shaped the Record Landscape

New Orleans was struck by two catastrophic fires before the target period began, and their consequences define what early 1800s researchers can and cannot find:

### 🔥 Great Fire of March 21, 1788
Destroyed approximately 856 buildings — the majority of the French Quarter — including colonial administrative archives. Much of the Spanish-era civil record infrastructure was lost.

### 🔥 Great Fire of December 8, 1794
A second fire destroyed approximately 212 more buildings, further cutting into surviving colonial records.

### 🌊 Chronic Flooding
New Orleans sits below sea level. Repeated flood events throughout the 1800s damaged or destroyed records held in lower-lying buildings. This is an ongoing risk that influenced where custodians stored duplicate and official records.

**Net effect for researchers:** Records generated *before* 1788 are largely lost. Records from 1788–1800 are incomplete and spotty. Records from 1800 onward are much better — but survival is uneven, and the fire losses mean you must lean heavily on substitute and surrogate sources rather than expecting complete civil registration.

> *Disaster survival information drawn from:* FamilySearch Wiki — "New Orleans Genealogy, Records Surviving Disasters" ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

---

## Records That Survived — and Where to Find Them

### 1. 🕍 St. Louis Cathedral Sacramental Registers (PRIMARY SUBSTITUTE for civil vital records)
**What they are:** Baptism, marriage, and burial registers maintained by St. Louis Cathedral, the Catholic parish for New Orleans.
**Date range:** From 1731 — predating civil registration by many decades — though with gaps caused by the 1788 and 1794 fires.
**Why they matter:** For the early 1800s, these registers are the closest thing to birth, marriage, and death records. Louisiana had **no statewide civil vital registration** during this period. The cathedral registers are the primary surviving record of vital events.
**Languages:** French and Latin; some Spanish-era entries in Spanish.
**Access:** Original registers are held at the **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives**. FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection ID 1612905, [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1612905)) covers this period and is **indexed + images** available online. This is one of your most searchable entry points.
**⚠️ Researcher warning:** Gaps exist due to fire losses; not every event was recorded. Entries are in French (and sometimes Spanish) — you must be able to read the original language or use a translator.

> *Source:* FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

---

### 2. 📜 Notarial Records (EXCEPTIONAL SURVIVAL — highest-value source)
**What they are:** Acts recorded before a notary public — the cornerstone of Louisiana's civil law system. Notarial acts documented sales, donations, mortgages, manumissions, marriage contracts, successions, business partnerships, wills, and nearly every significant legal transaction.
**Date range surviving:** From 1734; the **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** holds **over 30 million pages** of notarial acts.
**Why they survived:** Notaries were legally required to keep duplicate registers, and the archives maintained off-site copies. The fires destroyed some offices but not all copies.
**Why they matter as substitutes:** When vital records were destroyed, notarial acts pick up the slack — a marriage contract recorded before a notary is a direct substitute for a marriage register entry; a succession act names heirs and family relationships; a manumission act names enslaved persons and enslavers.
**Access:**
- **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** — physical repository; [https://www.notarialarchives.org/](https://www.notarialarchives.org/)
- FamilySearch has digitized **1 browse-only volume** of surviving notarial act microfilm for Orleans Parish (Image Group 004990115), covering **1803–1820**, 167 images, in **French and English**. This volume is **0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable** — it must be browsed image by image. Access it through FamilySearch's image viewer.

> *Source:* FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters)); FamilySearch volume_search result

---

### 3. 🏛️ Cabildo Records (Spanish Colonial Governing Body)
**What they are:** Administrative and judicial records of the Cabildo, the Spanish colonial governing council of New Orleans.
**Date range:** Active through the Spanish period (ending ~1803); the records survived into American custody.
**Why they matter:** The Cabildo kept civil and legal records during Spanish rule — land grants, court proceedings, slave transactions, and municipal business. For families who were in New Orleans before 1803, these are the civil administrative substitute for missing civil registration.
**Access:** Holdings are primarily at the **Louisiana State Museum** (which operates from the Cabildo building itself in Jackson Square, New Orleans) and the **Louisiana State Archives** in Baton Rouge.

> *Source:* FamilySearch Wiki, New Orleans Genealogy ([https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_Orleans_Genealogy#Records_Surviving_Disasters))

---

### 4. ⚖️ Successions / Probate Records
**What they are:** Louisiana "successions" = probate. These documents name heirs, list estate assets (including enslaved persons), and establish family relationships.
**Access:** FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** (Collection ID 2078341, [https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2078341)) covers the target period and is **indexed + images** online — highly searchable. Physical originals are at the **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** and the **Louisiana State Archives**.

---

### 5. 📊 Census Records
**What survived:**
- **1810 U.S. Federal Census** — first federal census of Louisiana as a territory, then state. Available and indexed.
- **1820, 1830, 1840 U.S. Federal Censuses** — all available for Orleans Parish. Heads of household only; enslaved persons listed by age/sex groupings, not by name.
- **Louisiana State/Territorial Census** — a territorial census was conducted ca. 1805 and is a crucial substitute for the gap before federal coverage; check for its availability at the Louisiana State Archives.
- **⚠️ 1890 Federal Census** was largely destroyed by fire — not a concern for the early 1800s, but a warning for later research.

**Access:** Ancestry.com and FamilySearch both hold digitized, indexed copies of federal census records. NARA holds originals. ([https://www.archives.gov/](https://www.archives.gov/))

---

### 6. 🪖 Military Records
**Battle of New Orleans (1815):** Service records for War of 1812 soldiers — including Jean Lafitte's privateer forces and free men of color who fought — are at NARA and digitized on **Fold3** ([https://www.fold3.com/](https://www.fold3.com/)). These are valuable locator tools for men in New Orleans ca. 1814–1815.
**Access:** NARA, Fold3 (subscription), FamilySearch.

---

### 7. ⛪ Other Church Records
New Orleans had a significant Catholic population but also Protestant, Jewish, and free-colored congregations by the early 1800s.
- **St. Patrick's Church** (Irish Catholic, founded 1833) and other parishes began keeping separate registers as the city grew.
- **Congregation Gates of Mercy** (Dispersa de Israel congregation, founded 1828) — one of the earliest Jewish congregations in the U.S. south.
- **FamilySearch "Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925"** (Collection 1612905) covers multiple denominations and parishes.

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers
New Orleans had an active press from the early 1800s. Newspapers published **obituaries, legal notices (successions, land sales), and manumission advertisements**.
- **Louisiana Gazette** (founded 1804) and **Le Moniteur de la Louisiane** (French-language) are key early 1800s papers.
- **Access:** **Newspapers.com** ([https://www.newspapers.com/](https://www.newspapers.com/)) holds digitized Louisiana newspapers. Also check the **Louisiana Digital Library** ([https://louisianadigitallibrary.org/](https://louisianadigitallibrary.org/)) and the **Library of Congress Chronicling America** project.

---

### 9. 🪦 Cemetery Records
New Orleans's above-ground burial culture (due to the water table) created distinctive tomb and cemetery records.
- St. Louis Cemetery No. 1 (1789), No. 2 (1823), and No. 3 (1854) are the primary Catholic cemeteries for this period.
- **Find A Grave** ([https://www.findagrave.com/](https://www.findagrave.com/)) has volunteer-transcribed records for many New Orleans cemeteries.
- The **Save Our Cemeteries** organization maintains records for historic New Orleans cemeteries.

---

### 10. 🏠 Land Records
**What survived:** Land records fared better than vital records because duplicates were required and federal land offices maintained their own copies.
- **U.S. General Land Office (GLO) patents** — post-1803 federal land grants are searchable at [https://glorecords.blm.gov/](https://glorecords.blm.gov/).
- **Spanish land grants** — pre-1803 grants were validated by U.S. commissioners after the Louisiana Purchase. The **American State Papers: Public Lands** series documents this process and is freely available at [https://memory.loc.gov/](https://memory.loc.gov/).
- **Orleans Parish conveyance records** (deed books) — held at the **Orleans Parish Clerk of Court** and partially available through the **Louisiana State Archives**.
- FamilySearch collection **"Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984"** also captures some property transfers through succession records.

---

### 11. 🔗 Enslaved Persons and Free People of Color
New Orleans had one of the largest free Black populations in the antebellum South. Researchers tracing enslaved ancestors or free persons of color should look at:
- **Notarial records** — manumission acts, freedom papers, and slave sale records name individuals. The Notarial Archives are the most important repository.
- **St. Louis Cathedral registers** — baptized enslaved and free Black Catholics appear in the same sacramental registers as white parishioners.
- **Cabildo records** — slave court proceedings and freedom petitions (cartas de libertad) from the Spanish period.
- **Succession inventories** — enslaved persons are named in estate inventories within succession records.
- The **Louisiana State Archives** holds a growing digitization project focused on records of enslaved persons.

---

## FamilySearch Digitized Collections — Summary

| Collection | ID | Date Range | Status |

| Louisiana, Church Records, 1718–1925 | 1612905 | 1718–1925 | **Indexed + images** |
| Louisiana, Probate Records, 1756–1984 | 2078341 | 1756–1984 | **Indexed + images** |
| Louisiana, Statewide Death Index, 1819–1964 | 1543892 | 1819–1964 | **Index only** (no images) |

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **New Orleans Notarial Archives Research Center** | 30M+ pages of notarial acts from 1734 | In-person; [notarialarchives.org](https://www.notarialarchives.org/) |
| **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives** | St. Louis Cathedral registers and other parish records | By appointment |
| **Louisiana State Archives, Baton Rouge** | Territorial and state records, successions, land | In-person + some online |
| **Louisiana State Museum / Cabildo** | Spanish colonial Cabildo records | In-person |
| **Orleans Parish Civil District Court** | Succession (probate) case files | In-person |
| **NARA Southeast Region (Atlanta)** | Federal records: census, military, naturalization | In-person + online (Ancestry, Fold3) |

---

## Substitute Source Strategy — When Records Were Destroyed

| If you need… | And civil records are missing… | Use instead… |
|---|---|---|
| Birth proof | No civil registration pre-1850s | St. Louis Cathedral baptismal register (Collection 1612905); notarial acts naming children |
| Marriage proof | Fire gaps in registers | Notarial marriage contracts (Notarial Archives); St. Louis Cathedral marriage register |
| Death proof | Incomplete records | Succession filings; newspaper death notices; cemetery records (Find A Grave) |
| Relationships / family structure | Any gap | Succession inventories naming heirs; tutorship filings naming minor children; notarial family acts |
| Pre-1788 ancestors | Near-total loss | Spanish colonial Cabildo records; surviving church registers; American State Papers land claims |

---

## Research Quirks and Warnings

- **No statewide civil vital registration** existed in Louisiana during the early 1800s. The FamilySearch Wiki returned only generic content for the Louisiana Vital Records page — the FamilySearch Wiki did not return Louisiana-specific registration dates in this session. Church registers and notarial acts are your primary substitutes.
- **Language barrier:** Records through at least the 1830s are frequently in French (and sometimes Spanish). Budget for translation or learn basic French paleography before browsing originals.
- **"Parish" means county:** Louisiana uses "parish" (not "county") as its primary civil division. Orleans Parish = the jurisdiction encompassing New Orleans city.
- **Civil law terminology differs from common law:** Search for "succession," not "probate"; "tutorship," not "guardianship"; "act of sale," not "deed."
- **The 1803 jurisdictional break is clean:** Records before 1803 were created under Spanish or French authority; records from 1803 on were created under American territorial/state authority. You may need to search different repositories for ancestors who span that date.
- **Notarial browse-only volume (004990115):** The one FamilySearch digitized notarial volume for 1803–1820 is entirely unindexed and must be read image-by-image in French or English with no search capability. Allow significant time to browse its 167 images.
- **FamilySearch wiki gap:** The four wiki place pages (home, getting_started, online_records, research_tips) for Louisiana and the five specific Louisiana topic wiki pages all returned generic fallback content in this session — consult the FamilySearch Wiki directly at [https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Louisiana_Genealogy) for additional detail the tools did not surface.

---

Here's a concise summary of the most important points for your research:

**The fires of 1788 and 1794 are the defining disaster** — they destroyed most colonial archives, so for the early 1800s you're working with what survived or was re-created afterward. The good news is that three record systems largely survived and are exceptional substitutes:

1. **St. Louis Cathedral sacramental registers** (baptisms/marriages/burials from 1731 with gaps) — the closest thing to vital records; indexed on FamilySearch in Collection 1612905.
2. **Notarial acts** — Louisiana's civil law system required notarization of nearly every major life event, and duplicate registers protected them; the New Orleans Notarial Archives holds 30M+ pages from 1734, with one browse-only FamilySearch volume covering 1803–1820.
3. **Cabildo / succession records** — Spanish colonial administrative records and Louisiana probate (succession) records survived well; FamilySearch Collection 2078341 covers probate from 1756 onward with indexed images.

For enslaved ancestors and free people of color, the notarial records and St. Louis Cathedral registers are indispensable — New Orleans's free Black community was large and documented in both systems. The key physical repositories are the **Notarial Archives Research Center**, the **Archdiocese of New Orleans Archives**, the **Louisiana State Archives in Baton Rouge**, and the **Louisiana State Museum/Cabildo**.

# Port of Boston — Immigration Records, 1840s
**Locality Research Guide**
**Place:** Boston, Suffolk, Massachusetts, United States
**Time period:** 1840–1849
**Focus:** Tracing immigrants entering through the Port of Boston

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Boston was one of the five busiest U.S. ports of entry in the 1840s, receiving tens of thousands of immigrants — above all Irish families fleeing the Great Famine (1845–1852). By 1850 more than a quarter of Boston's residents were Irish-born (Wikipedia). Arrivals were recorded in customs passenger lists maintained under federal authority at the Port of Boston (National Archives Record Group 36). Massachusetts recorded vital events at the **town level** during this period; the Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey, so consult it directly at https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records for authoritative town- and state-level registration dates.

---

## Record Classes

### 1. ⭐ Passenger / Arrival Lists — PRIMARY SOURCE

**What they contain:** Customs passenger lists required by the federal Passenger Acts record name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin. Unlike later Ellis Island manifests, 1840s lists do **not** typically include hometown, last residence, or a U.S. contact — do not expect a specific village name from the manifest alone.

**FamilySearch — indexed collection:**
- **Massachusetts, Passenger Lists, 1820–1891** (collection 1784312, date range 1820–1891)
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1784312

**Digitized volume found by volume_search:**
| Image Group | Coverage | Images | % Name-Indexed | Full-Text Searchable |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **003345210** | Port of Boston Passenger Lists, 1840–1850 | 389 | **3%** | ✅ Yes |

Because only 3% of this volume is name-indexed, a standard record search will miss the vast majority of entries. **Use full-text search first; if no match, browse image-by-image through all 389 images.** `volume_search` returned 1 total result for migration record types in this window — additional volumes may exist under other record-type groupings.

**Originals:** National Archives at Boston, Waltham, MA (NARA Record Group 36).
**Also indexed on:** Ancestry.com U.S. Passenger Lists collections.

*Source: [Massachusetts Immigration — Port of Boston](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Immigration#Port_of_Boston)*

---

### 2. Naturalization Records

**What they contain:** Before 1906, any court of record — federal, state, or local — could naturalize an immigrant. The two-step process (declaration of intent, then petition for naturalization) was often spread years apart. Many 1840s arrivals did not naturalize until the 1850s–1860s; search a 10–20-year window around the arrival date.

**FamilySearch — indexed collection:**
- **Massachusetts, Naturalization Records, 1790–1906** (collection 1459213)
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1459213

**Key courts:** Boston Municipal Court, U.S. District Court for Massachusetts (Suffolk County). Originals at the National Archives at Boston (Waltham).

---

### 3. Church Records — Essential for Irish Immigrants

**What they contain:** Catholic parish registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) often predate and supplement civil vital registration. For Irish Famine-era immigrants, these are frequently the best source for vital events and family structure.

**FamilySearch — indexed collection:**
- **Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920** (collection 1921657)
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657

**Key Boston parishes for Irish immigrants** (per FamilySearch Wiki search result):
- Cathedral of the Holy Cross
- St. Patrick's Church

The **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** holds registers for many parishes from the 1840s onward.

*Source: [Massachusetts Church Records — Boston Area](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Boston)*

---

### 4. Town Vital Records

**What they contain:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded at the Boston/town level.

**FamilySearch — indexed collection:**
- **Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890** (collection 2061550)
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550

**Note:** The Massachusetts Vital Records wiki page returned only generic content in this survey. Consult https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Vital_Records directly for the specific years town-level registration was required and when statewide registration followed.

---

### 5. Probate Records

**What they contain:** Wills, estate inventories, and administration files. For immigrant ancestors, estate files may name relatives in the home country and provide details unavailable elsewhere.

**FamilySearch — indexed collection:**
- **Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991** (collection 1678901)
  https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901

**Repository:** Suffolk County Probate Court, Boston.

---

### 6. Federal Census

The **1840 census** lists only the head of household by name. The **1850 census** was the first to list every household member individually — it is critical for locating an immigrant family in the years just after arrival. Mortality schedules (1850–1885) capture deaths in the year before the census and may document recently arrived immigrants who died shortly after landing.

**Access:** FamilySearch (free); Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/).

---

### 7. Newspapers — The Pilot's "Information Wanted" Columns

**The Boston Pilot** (Irish Catholic newspaper) published "Information Wanted" advertisements — missing-persons notices placed by relatives seeking separated family members. This is an extraordinary and often overlooked finding aid specific to Irish Famine-era immigration. Boston College has digitized this database.

General historical Boston newspapers are available at **Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/).

---

### 8. Military Records

If the immigrant or his sons served in the Civil War (1861–1865 — just one decade after arrival), pension files at NARA are rich with biographical data: place of birth, U.S. arrival date, and names of relatives.

**Access:** Fold3 (https://www.fold3.com/); National Archives (https://www.archives.gov/).

---

### 9. Cemetery Records

**Access:** Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) — useful for establishing death dates and grouping family members buried together.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **National Archives at Boston** (Waltham, MA) | Passenger lists (RG 36), naturalization records | In-person; microfilm/digital via NARA |
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Indexed passenger lists, vitals, church records, naturalization | Free online |
| **Ancestry.com** | Passenger lists, census, naturalization | Subscription |
| **Archdiocese of Boston Archives** | Catholic parish registers from 1840s onward | Contact for access |
| **Massachusetts State Archives** (Boston) | State-level records, alien registers | In-person |
| **Boston City Archives** | City vital records | In-person |

---

## Critical Quirks

1. **1840s passenger list data is sparse** — name, age, sex, occupation, and country of origin only. No hometown or village. To establish the origin community, corroborate with church records, naturalization files, and civil registration in the home country.

2. **Volume 003345210 is only 3% name-indexed.** Standard name search will miss ~97% of entries. Always supplement with full-text search and, if necessary, image-by-image browsing across all 389 images.

3. **Naturalizations are scattered across multiple courts** before 1906 — search Suffolk County courts, the U.S. District Court, and any court in towns where the immigrant later settled.

4. **Also check New York passenger lists.** Some immigrants listed Boston as destination but landed in New York, and vice versa. Covering both ports reduces the chance of a miss.

5. **The Boston Pilot "Information Wanted" database is a unique Irish-immigration finding aid** — check it before assuming an immigrant left no trace.

6. **The Massachusetts Vital Records, Suffolk County Genealogy, and Massachusetts Immigration wiki pages returned only generic content** in this survey session. Visit those pages directly on the FamilySearch Wiki for authoritative, jurisdiction-specific guidance on registration dates and record availability.

Here is the locality research guide based on everything the tools returned.

---

# Locality Research Guide
## Indian Territory (present-day Oklahoma) · Mid-1800s · Native American Tribal Research

---

### Jurisdictional Context

In the mid-1800s, the land now called Oklahoma was designated **Indian Territory** — a distinct federal jurisdiction, not a U.S. state or organized territory. The Five Civilized Tribes (Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Muscogee/Creek, and Seminole) were forcibly relocated there under the Indian Removal Act of 1830, arriving primarily through the 1830s–1840s. Each nation maintained its own tribal government, courts, and records. Oklahoma did not achieve statehood until **1907**, meaning:

- **No county-level civil registration** existed during the mid-1800s
- **No statewide vital records** system applied (the FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma Vital Records returned only generic content — no specific registration start date could be confirmed from returned tool results; consult the Oklahoma Historical Society directly for this)
- The **federal Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA)** and tribal governments were the primary record-keepers
- Records may appear under **"Indian Territory"** rather than "Oklahoma" in databases — search both

FamilySearch has **4 indexed collections** and **1 digitized volume** confirmed for this jurisdiction and period; the four wiki_place_page sections all resolved to generic guidance (not Oklahoma-specific), which is a coverage gap noted below.

---

### 1. Tribal Enrollment Records — **Highest Priority**

#### Dawes Rolls (1898–1914)
Though slightly after your target window, these are the **most important records** for tracing Five Civilized Tribes ancestry. They list name, age, sex, blood quantum, and tribal affiliation, and enrollment applications often reference birth dates and parents reaching well into the mid-1800s.

- **Held at:** National Archives, Southwest Region, Fort Worth, Texas
- **Online:** Indexed at FamilySearch and Ancestry.com
- **FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* — searchable, with images

#### Pre-Dawes Rolls (directly in-period)
The wiki search confirmed these earlier rolls:
- **Old Settler Cherokee Roll (1851)** — names Cherokees already in Indian Territory before the main removal
- **Drennen Roll (1852)** — Cherokee
- Various tribal census rolls maintained by each tribal nation's government throughout the 1850s–1890s

These are included within FamilySearch's **"Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** collection.

#### Digitized Volume Confirmed by FamilySearch
| Volume | Images | Indexed | Full-text | Access |
|--------|--------|---------|-----------|--------|
| Tribal Enrollment Cards, Indian Territory, 1840–1870 (Image Group 002298871) | 940 | 99% | Yes | Indexed + full-text searchable on FamilySearch |

This is the only volume volume_search returned for the Indigenous record type in this period. It is 99% name-indexed and full-text searchable — start here.

---

### 2. Land & Allotment Records — **Indexed + Images**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907*
- Date range: 1834–1907 (spans your entire target window)
- Held and searchable on FamilySearch

Land records in Indian Territory operated differently from standard federal land states. Tribal lands were held communally; individual allotments came primarily through the Dawes Act (1887) and the work of the Dawes Commission. Pre-allotment land use is reflected in BIA agency correspondence and tribal council records. The BLM General Land Office (glorecords.blm.gov) also holds some Indian Territory patents.

---

### 3. Mission & Church Records — **Indexed + Images**

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965*
- Date range: 1820–1965 — covers your target period fully
- Searchable on FamilySearch

The wiki search confirmed that Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Moravian missionaries were active among relocated tribes from the 1820s onward, keeping registers of converts, students, and community members. These records are often the **only source for vital events** (births, marriages, deaths) in Indian Territory during the mid-1800s, given the absence of civil registration. Denominational archives (e.g., American Baptist Historical Society, Presbyterian Historical Society) may hold originals not yet digitized.

---

### 4. Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Agency Records — **Physical / Microfilm at NARA**

The BIA maintained extensive records for each tribal agency in Indian Territory, including:
- **Annuity payment rolls** — list heads of household by name and family size, year by year
- **Census rolls** — periodic tribal censuses conducted by BIA agents
- **Correspondence files** — name individuals in disputes, land matters, and family situations
- **School records** — for the Indian boarding schools in Indian Territory

**Held at:** National Archives, Southwest Region, **Fort Worth, Texas** (RG 75 — Records of the Bureau of Indian Affairs). This is your primary physical repository.
**Online access:** Fold3 (fold3.com) has digitized some BIA records; Ancestry.com holds others. NARA's online catalog (catalog.archives.gov) lists what is available for request.

---

### 5. Treaty Documents

Treaty records document the legal relationship between the U.S. government and each tribe, including signatories (tribal leaders) and terms affecting families (land cessions, annuities, citizenship rights). These are **federal records** held at:
- **NARA Washington, D.C.** (RG 11 — General Records of the U.S. Government, ratified treaties)
- **NARA Fort Worth** (agency-level treaty correspondence)
- Published in *Kappler's Indian Affairs: Laws and Treaties* — fully digitized at the Oklahoma State University digital library (digital.library.okstate.edu/kappler)

---

### 6. Tribal Nation Archives — **Do Not Overlook**

Each of the Five Civilized Tribes maintains its own archives, separate from NARA:

| Nation | Archive |
|--------|---------|
| Cherokee Nation | Cherokee Nation Cultural Resource Center, Tahlequah, OK |
| Choctaw Nation | Choctaw Nation of Oklahoma, Durant, OK |
| Chickasaw Nation | Chickasaw Nation Archives & Library, Ada, OK |
| Muscogee (Creek) Nation | Muscogee Nation Library/Archives, Okmulgee, OK |
| Seminole Nation | Seminole Nation Museum, Wewoka, OK |

These hold tribal court records, citizenship rolls, council minutes, and records not held anywhere else.

---

### 7. Federal Census Records — **Indexed**

Indian Territory households were **not included** in the standard federal decennial census until later periods. However:
- **Indian census schedules** (separate from the general population schedules) were taken periodically under BIA authority
- The 1880 federal census included some Indian Territory enumeration
- Mortality schedules (1850–1885) may name tribal individuals who died in the year preceding each census

FamilySearch's *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* covers the tribal census series.

---

### 8. Marriage Records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (date range begins 1890 — post-target for most mid-1800s research). For the mid-1800s, marriage records exist primarily in:
- **Tribal court records** (held at tribal archives and NARA Fort Worth)
- **Mission/church registers** (the FamilySearch Mission and Church Records collection above)

---

### 9. Military Records

The Five Civilized Tribes raised both Union and Confederate units during the Civil War (1861–1865), producing service records and pension files relevant to the 1860s:
- **Fold3** (fold3.com) — indexed Civil War service records
- **NARA, Washington D.C.** (RG 94, RG 109) — Confederate and Union service records

---

### Key Repositories at a Glance

| Repository | What It Holds | Access |
|---|---|---|
| NARA Southwest Region, Fort Worth, TX | BIA agency records, tribal census rolls, Dawes enrollment files | Physical + some digitized on Ancestry/Fold3 |
| FamilySearch (familysearch.org) | Indian Censuses & Rolls, Land Records, Mission Records, Tribal Enrollment Cards | Free online, indexed |
| Oklahoma Historical Society (okhistory.org) | Oklahoma territorial records, newspapers, photographs | Physical + some online |
| Individual tribal archives (see above) | Tribal court records, citizenship rolls, council minutes | Contact each tribe directly |
| Ancestry.com | Dawes Rolls, BIA records, federal censuses | Subscription |
| Fold3 (fold3.com) | Military and some BIA records | Subscription |
| BLM GLO (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents | Free online |
| OSU Digital Library (digital.library.okstate.edu/kappler) | Kappler's treaties, digitized in full | Free online |

---

### Researcher Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Search under "Indian Territory," not just "Oklahoma"** — FamilySearch and Ancestry both use "Indian Territory" as a jurisdiction label for pre-1907 records. If you search only "Oklahoma," you will miss the bulk of mid-1800s records.
2. **The Dawes Rolls are post-1898 but essential** — Even for mid-1800s ancestors, the Dawes enrollment application files record parents' names, ages, and tribal affiliations going back a generation. Work backward from Dawes to the earlier rolls.
3. **Freedmen rolls are separate** — Formerly enslaved people of tribal members were enrolled in separate "Freedmen" rolls within the Dawes series. If your ancestor may have been enslaved by a tribal member, search the Freedmen roll specifically.
4. **Tribal members had both English and Native names** — Search databases under both; the same individual may appear differently across records.
5. **No county courts in Indian Territory** — Tribal courts held jurisdiction over tribal members in civil and criminal matters. Those records are at tribal archives and NARA Fort Worth, not county courthouses.
6. **The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Oklahoma returned only generic content** — The specific Oklahoma wiki pages (Oklahoma Native Americans, Oklahoma Vital Records, Dawes Rolls, Indian Territory Genealogy) all resolved to a generic page rather than subject-specific guidance. Consult the FamilySearch Wiki manually at familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Native_American_Records for richer guidance.
7. **Pre-removal records** — For families of the Five Civilized Tribes, records from their original homelands (Georgia, Alabama, Mississippi, Tennessee, Florida) from before the 1830s–1840s removal exist in southeastern state archives and NARA, and may be needed to trace families back further than the Indian Territory period.

---

### Recommended Starting Sequence

1. Search **FamilySearch "Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959"** for your ancestor's name and tribe
2. Search the **Tribal Enrollment Cards volume (Image Group 002298871)** on FamilySearch — 940 images, 99% indexed
3. Search **Dawes Roll applications** on Ancestry or FamilySearch to identify the family cluster and get birth/parent data pointing back to the mid-1800s
4. Pull the corresponding **BIA agency annuity rolls and census rolls** at NARA Fort Worth (or request digitized copies through Ancestry/Fold3)
5. Contact the **relevant tribal archive** for court, citizenship, and council records not held federally
6. Search **FamilySearch Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965** for baptisms, marriages, and burials
