---

# Locality Guide: Massachusetts, United States — Early Puritan Settlements (c. 1620–1692)

## Jurisdiction overview

- **Period covered:** Two overlapping colonial jurisdictions — **Plymouth Colony** (1620–1691) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628–1691) — both merged into the **Province of Massachusetts Bay** in 1691/1692
- **Governance model:** Town-meeting government; county structure established in Massachusetts Bay Colony in 1643 (Suffolk, Essex, Middlesex, Norfolk Counties). Plymouth Colony established Plymouth County and Bristol County in 1685
- **Population:** Approximately 20,000 English settlers arrived during the Great Migration of 1630–1640, according to Wikipedia. No population figures were returned by the population data tool for this period
- **Economy:** Subsistence farming, fishing, timber, and maritime trade
- **Ethnic/religious composition:** Predominantly English Puritan (Congregationalist). Plymouth settlers included Separatist Pilgrims. Quakers arrived after 1656; Anglicans present in some coastal towns
- **Language of records:** English throughout; Latin occasionally in church contexts
- **Key historical events:** Pequot War (1636–1638), King Philip's War (1675–1678), Salem Witch Trials (1692)

---

## Boundary changes

This is the most important jurisdictional complexity for this period:

- **Plymouth Colony** (1620–1691) and **Massachusetts Bay Colony** (1628–1691) were entirely **separate jurisdictions**. Families in Plymouth, Duxbury, Marshfield, Taunton, or other Plymouth Colony towns generated records under a completely different colonial government than families in Boston, Salem, Cambridge, or Ipswich
- The two colonies **merged in 1691** into the Province of Massachusetts Bay. From 1692 onward, records are unified under one provincial government
- **Norfolk County (1643):** The original Norfolk County (covering what is now southern New Hampshire) was dissolved in 1679; its records moved to Essex County — search Essex County for families who lived in towns like Haverhill, Salisbury, or Hampton before 1679
- **York County (1652):** Covered territory that is now the state of Maine. Maine families during this period fall under Massachusetts Bay Colony jurisdiction; York County, Massachusetts, United States records are a separate research trail
- **Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately** and must be researched as a distinct body from Massachusetts Bay Colony records ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Always identify which colony your ancestor lived in before searching. A Boston ancestor (Massachusetts Bay Colony) and a Plymouth ancestor (Plymouth Colony) require entirely different record searches, even though both are within modern Massachusetts.

---

## Available record types

### Vital records (civil registration)

- **Start date — town level:** The colony mandated that towns record births, marriages, and deaths **beginning in 1639**, making Massachusetts one of the earliest civil registration jurisdictions in North America ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Holding level:** **Town** — not county. Records were created and held at the town clerk level, not the county. Always search by the specific town, not the county
- **What exists:** Births, marriages, and deaths recorded in town clerk books from 1639 onward. Pre-1639 events are not civilly registered; rely on church records for those years
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Town Vital Records, 1620–1890"** (collection [2061550](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2061550)) — **indexed + images** — covers the full target period
- **Published compilations:** The multi-volume *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* series (known as the Tanner–Corbin series) abstracts town clerk records for over 200 Massachusetts towns and is widely available in research libraries and at NEHGS ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))
- **Gaps:** Pre-1639 births, marriages, and deaths have no civil registration — church records are the sole alternative. Some early town records are incomplete or lost
- **Plymouth Colony alternative:** Plymouth Colony vital records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately from Massachusetts Bay Colony town records

---

### Church records

**The single most important record type for early Puritan Massachusetts.** The Congregational meeting was the established church of the colony and kept the most detailed records.

- **Denominations present:** Congregationalist (Puritan/Puritan Separatist) dominant; also Baptist (after 1630s), Quaker (after 1656, though heavily persecuted), Anglican
- **Record types:** Church membership lists, baptismal registers, marriage records, burial records, and disciplinary proceedings (excommunications, admonishments) — the latter often naming family members and providing relationship information ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Church Records, 1630–1920"** (collection [1921657](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1921657)) — **indexed + images**
- **Digitized volume:** **Volume 007612045** — 121 images of Suffolk County Congregational church admissions and baptisms, 1630–1700 — **full-text searchable but NOT name-indexed** (search by keyword/full-text; cannot do a standard name search)
- **Published records:** Many early church records are published in the *Colonial Society of Massachusetts* series and in local historical society publications ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Language:** English

---

### Census records

- **Federal census:** Does not begin until 1790 — **no federal census records exist for this period**
- **State/colonial enumeration:** No systematic territorial census during 1620–1692
- **Substitutes:** Town meeting records and tax/rate lists serve as population substitutes. FamilySearch has digitized town meeting and proprietors' records — see below under Land Records. Tax lists and militia muster rolls (Massachusetts Archives) enumerate adult males

---

### Probate and court records

- **Date range:** County-level probate courts began operating in the **1630s** in Massachusetts Bay Colony ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))
- **Holding level:** County probate courts
- **FamilySearch collection:** **"Massachusetts, Probate Records, 1635–1991"** (collection [1678901](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1678901)) — **indexed + images** — begins directly within the target period
- **Types:** Wills (testate), administrations (intestate), guardianships, estate inventories — inventories from this period are especially rich in detail about household goods, livestock, and property
- **Courts of Assistants:** The General Court (colonial legislature) doubled as a high court and handled major civil and criminal cases; its records are at the Massachusetts Archives
- **Plymouth Colony:** Plymouth Colony court records are published and available separately

---

### Land records

- **Survey system:** Metes and bounds (Massachusetts is a state-land state — no federal land patents apply)
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** Original land grants were issued by town proprietors (groups of original settlers), not the colonial government directly. Town proprietors' records document original grants and divisions
- **Holding level:** County (deeds recorded at county registries of deeds from the 1630s) and town (proprietors' records)
- **FamilySearch digitized volume:** **Volume 007612044** — 188 images of Massachusetts town meeting and proprietors' records, 1620–1698 — **browse-only** (0% indexed, not full-text searchable — must be browsed image by image)
- **Where held:** Original deed books are at the county registries of deeds; the Massachusetts Archives holds additional colonial land records. FamilySearch has microfilmed many deed books but most for this early period are browse-only
- **Types:** Deeds, grants, patents, proprietors' divisions, and town meeting votes on land allocation
- **Note:** Land records in early Massachusetts often name neighbors, relatives, and witnesses — rich for relationship evidence

---

### Military records

- **Relevant conflicts:**
  - **Pequot War (1636–1638):** First major conflict; militia muster rolls exist
  - **King Philip's War (1675–1678):** The most destructive war per capita in American history; extensive militia records, prisoner lists, and land confiscation records
- **Record types:** Colonial militia muster rolls, impressment lists, pension petitions (rare for this period), and court records relating to service obligations
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives (Boston) holds the primary colonial military records. Published rosters appear in state historical society volumes. NARA (archives.gov) holds some later records but colonial-era records are primarily at the state level
- **Fold3** (fold3.com) covers some early military records; coverage of the 1620–1692 period is limited compared to later conflicts

---

### Cemetery records

- **Major early cemeteries:** Burying grounds attached to town commons (e.g., Granary Burying Ground, Boston, 1660; King's Chapel Burying Ground, Boston, 1630; Charter Street Cemetery, Salem, 1637)
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave (findagrave.com) indexes many early New England burying grounds with transcriptions and photographs, though coverage is volunteer-driven and uneven for 17th-century stones
- **Physical records:** Sexton records are sparse for this early period; the gravestones themselves are often the primary record. The Association for Gravestone Studies (northampton.edu/ags) specializes in early New England grave markers

---

### Newspaper records

- **Coverage during period:** The first Massachusetts newspaper, *Publick Occurrences* (1690), published only one issue before being suppressed. The *Boston News-Letter* began in 1704 — **no newspapers circulated in Massachusetts during most of the 1620–1692 window**
- **Value:** Not applicable as a primary source for this period

---

### Immigration / emigration records

- **The Great Migration (1630–1640):** Approximately 20,000 English settlers arrived, documented comprehensively in the NEHGS *Great Migration* study series (every known settler arriving 1620–1643 is profiled with sources cited)
- **17th-century passenger lists:** Systematic passenger manifests do not exist for this era as they do for the 19th century. The FamilySearch "Massachusetts, Passenger Lists" collection (1784312) begins in 1820 and **does not cover the colonial period**
- **Key resource:** The *Great Migration* series at NEHGS is the closest equivalent to an arrival index for this period; many volumes are digitized at AmericanAncestors.org

---

### Tax records

- **Types:** Colonial rate lists (property tax assessments) and poll tax lists; town-level
- **Date range:** Rate lists survive from the 1640s onward for many towns
- **Where held:** Massachusetts Archives and town clerk records; some published by local historical societies
- **Substitute value:** Rate lists enumerate adult males and property holders — an important substitute for census records during this period when no census existed

---

## Repository guide

### Online repositories

| Repository | Collections for this place | Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | Town Vital Records 1620–1890 (indexed + images); Church Records 1630–1920 (indexed + images); Probate Records 1635–1991 (indexed + images); plus 2 digitized browse/full-text volumes (007612044, 007612045) | Free |
| **AmericanAncestors.org** (NEHGS) | Great Migration study series; manuscript collections; compiled genealogies; NEHGS Register | Subscription / some free |
| **FindAGrave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery transcriptions for early New England burying grounds | Free |
| **Fold3** (fold3.com) | Some colonial-era military records; limited for 1620–1692 | Subscription |
| **National Archives** (archives.gov) | Colonial-era records held federally are sparse; primary colonial records are at Massachusetts Archives | Free catalog; some digital |

**Coverage of this survey:** `volume_search` returned 2 digitized volumes matching Massachusetts for 1620–1700 — this is the **complete result set** (totalResults: 2, no further pages). The FamilySearch indexed collections (Town Vital Records, Church Records, Probate Records) represent separately catalogued indexed collections not reflected in the volume count.

> **Note on external links:** The `external_links_search` tool returned 6 results but the query did not resolve to a Massachusetts-specific place ID — the returned links (Ancestry census collection, Find A Grave, Newspapers.com, Fold3, NARA) are generic U.S. genealogy resources, not curated Massachusetts-specific links. Treat them as general-purpose starting points, not a verified list of Massachusetts-specific holdings.

### Physical repositories

| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| **Massachusetts Archives** (Boston) | Original colony records from the 1620s, governor's correspondence, court records, colonial military records, colonial land records | In-person; some records digitized |
| **New England Historic Genealogical Society (NEHGS)** (Boston) | Largest genealogical library in New England; manuscript collections, published genealogies, Great Migration series | In-person research library; remote services via AmericanAncestors.org |
| **County Registries of Deeds** (each county) | Deed books from the 1630s (county established); remarkably complete runs ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational)) | In-person; some counties digitized online |
| **County Probate Courts** (each county) | Probate files from the 1630s onward | In-person; many microfilmed by FamilySearch |
| **Town Clerk Offices** (each town) | Original town meeting minutes, vital records, and proprietors' records | In-person; many abstracted in published series |
| **Pilgrim Hall Museum** (Plymouth) | Plymouth Colony–specific records and documents | In-person; some online |

---

## Records NOT online

- **Most town meeting minutes and proprietors' records:** Only 2 digitized volumes appear in FamilySearch for this period; the vast majority of town-level records must be consulted at the town clerk's office, Massachusetts Archives, or in published abstracts
- **Colonial court records (Courts of Assistants, General Court):** Available at the Massachusetts Archives; some published but not broadly digitized
- **Colonial militia records (outside major conflicts):** Primarily physical at Massachusetts Archives
- **Early Anglican church records:** Not widely digitized for this period
- **Quaker meeting records:** Held at New England Yearly Meeting archives (Providence, RI); not broadly digitized for the 17th century
- **Rate lists (tax records):** Largely physical at town clerk offices or Massachusetts Archives; some published by local historical societies

---

## Known record losses

- **King Philip's War (1675–1678):** Several towns were burned — Brookfield, Deerfield, Lancaster, Medfield, and others — and their town records were destroyed with the settlements. Survivors often resettled elsewhere, making record continuity difficult. Look for survivors in other towns' records
- **Early town records generally:** Pre-1639 vital events have no civil registration at all; gaps in early town clerk books are common due to fire, flood, and neglect. Published abstracts sometimes preserve records no longer held by the town
- **Plymouth Colony:** Some Plymouth Colony records were lost or damaged; however, *Plymouth Colony Records* (12 volumes, ed. Nathaniel Shurtleff) is the primary published source and covers 1620–1691

---

## Research tips

1. **Identify the colony first.** Determine whether your ancestor lived under Plymouth Colony (southeastern Massachusetts — Plymouth, Barnstable, Bristol counties) or Massachusetts Bay Colony (the rest) before choosing where to search. These were separate governments with separate record systems until 1691. Plymouth Colony records (1620–1691) are published and indexed separately ([Massachusetts Church Records — Congregational](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Church_Records#Congregational))

2. **Search by town, not county.** Vital records in early Massachusetts are held at the **town level**. Search the specific town in the FamilySearch "Town Vital Records" collection (2061550), not at the county level ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

3. **Start with the NEHGS Great Migration study series.** If your ancestor arrived between 1620 and 1643, this series (available at AmericanAncestors.org) profiles every known settler with cited source lists — it is the fastest entry point into early Massachusetts research ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

4. **Use the published *Vital Records* series.** The Tanner–Corbin *Vital Records of [Town Name] to 1850* abstracts (200+ towns) are available in many genealogical libraries and often at FamilySearch and Internet Archive. They index records that are now difficult to read in the original

5. **Church records can pre-date civil registration.** For events before 1639 — or where the town vital record is missing — Congregational church registers are the primary substitute. The FamilySearch Church Records collection (1921657) covers 1630 onward; Volume 007612045 is full-text searchable for Suffolk County church admissions and baptisms 1630–1700

6. **Probate inventories are genealogically rich.** 17th-century Massachusetts estate inventories list household members, debts owed by neighbors (often relatives), and tools that indicate occupation. The FamilySearch Probate Records collection (1678901) begins in 1635

7. **Volume 007612044 (town meeting/proprietors' records) must be browsed image by image** — it is 0% name-indexed and not full-text searchable. Use it when you know the specific town and approximate date range

8. **Check adjoining counties for early Norfolk County.** If your family lived in Haverhill, Salisbury, Amesbury, or Newbury before 1679, those records were created under the original Norfolk County and transferred to Essex County when Norfolk was dissolved. Search Essex County for pre-1679 records of these towns

9. **King Philip's War survivors may appear in other towns.** Families from burned towns (Brookfield, Lancaster, Deerfield, etc.) relocated; look in neighboring town records for survivors after 1675

10. **The Massachusetts Archives is the anchor repository** for colonial records not available online — the original colony records, governor's correspondence, and court records run from the 1620s onward ([Massachusetts Genealogy — Colonial Vital Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Massachusetts_Genealogy#Colonial_Vital_Records))

## 🗺️ Oklahoma Territory Locality Research Guide — 1889–1910

### Jurisdictional Context

Oklahoma's territorial period is one of the most complex in American genealogy because **two separate jurisdictions coexisted** until statehood:

| Jurisdiction | Dates | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Unassigned Lands** | Pre-April 22, 1889 | No organized civil government; sparse records |
| **Oklahoma Territory** | May 2, 1890 – Nov. 16, 1907 | Organic Act; capital at Guthrie |
| **Indian Territory** | Concurrent 1889–1907 | Five Civilized Tribes; separate administration |
| **State of Oklahoma** | November 16, 1907 onward | Both territories merged |

> ⚠️ **Critical quirk:** Determine which territory your ancestor lived in *before* choosing where to search. Oklahoma Territory (organized) and Indian Territory (Five Civilized Tribes administration) generated entirely different record sets, held at different repositories. Searching only one side will miss the other.

The Land Run of 1889 (April 22) opened approximately two million acres to ~50,000 settlers at noon. Homestead claims were filed at land offices in **Guthrie** and **Kingfisher**. Subsequent land runs in **1891, 1892, 1893, and 1895** opened additional areas — your ancestor may have arrived in a later run, not the famous first one.

Many Land Run settlers came from **Kansas, Texas, and Missouri** — tracing origins often requires searching departure-state records. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))

---

### Record-by-Record Survey

---

#### 🏡 1. Land Records *(Prime Source for This Period)*
**Digitization level: Partially indexed + images**

The homestead process generated some of the richest genealogical records of the era. Each file typically includes the original application, proof of settlement with named witnesses, and the final land patent. **Rejected applications also survive** and often contain family details. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Land Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run))

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma and Indian Territory, Early Land Records, 1834–1907* (Collection [1541872](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1541872)) | Online, name-searchable | 234,567 records, 117,283 images |
| **FamilySearch digitized volume** — Land-entry case files / homestead final proofs (Image Group 005221388) | Online — **74% name-indexed** | 402 images; 1889–1907; reachable via record search |
| **BLM General Land Office Records** — glorecords.blm.gov | Free online | Land patents searchable by name; downloadable images |
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** — Record Group 49 (General Land Office) | Physical + some digitized | Original case files for homestead proofs |

> 💡 **Start here.** A homestead final proof is often the earliest document placing a family in Oklahoma, and names witnesses who may be neighbors or kin.

---

#### 🪶 2. Indian Territory / Five Civilized Tribes Records
**Digitization level: Indexed collection + browse-only images (Dawes jackets)**

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Indian Censuses and Rolls, 1851–1959* (Collection [1987432](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1987432)) | Online, name-searchable | 567,890 records, 283,945 images |
| **FamilySearch digitized volume** — Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (Image Group 005221389) | Online — **BROWSE-ONLY** (0% indexed) | 176 images; 1898–1910; must be searched image-by-image with no name index |

> ⚠️ The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets are **browse-only images** — there is no name index, and full-text search is not available. You must page through them manually. These enrollment records were required for citizenship in the Five Civilized Tribes and contain detailed family information.

The Dawes rolls and the earlier tribal censuses are the fundamental sources for families in Indian Territory. NARA at Fort Worth also holds extensive Five Civilized Tribes records.

---

#### 💍 3. Marriage Records
**Digitization level: Indexed + images**

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, County Marriages, 1890–1995* (Collection [2134789](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2134789)) | Online, name-searchable | 456,789 records, 913,578 persons, 228,394 images |

County-level marriage registration began as counties were organized in Oklahoma Territory following the 1890 Organic Act. This collection's 1890 start date aligns closely with when county infrastructure was established.

---

#### ⛪ 4. Church / Mission Records
**Digitization level: Indexed + images (FamilySearch collection); physical for newer records**

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** — *Oklahoma, Mission and Church Records, 1820–1965* (Collection [1654321](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1654321)) | Online, name-searchable | 123,456 records, 61,728 images |
| **Denominational archives** | Physical | Check Baptist, Methodist, Presbyterian, and Catholic mission records |

Church records begin **sporadically in 1889** as denominations established congregations in new towns. ([FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)) Mission records are particularly important for Indian Territory families.

---

#### 📋 5. Census Records
**Digitization level: Indexed (federal) + physical/microfilm (1890 territorial)**

| Census | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **1890 Oklahoma Territory Special Census** | **Oklahoma Historical Society** (physical/microfilm) | ⭐ One of the **very few surviving 1890 census records** in the nation — most of the 1890 federal census was destroyed. Critical substitute. ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Land_Records#Land_Run)) |
| **1900 Federal Census** | Ancestry.com, FamilySearch — name-indexed | Covers Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory in separate schedules |
| **1910 Federal Census** | Ancestry.com, FamilySearch — name-indexed | First post-statehood enumeration |
| **Territorial tax rolls, 1890s** | Oklahoma State Archives | County-level; help document early settlers between enumerations ([FamilySearch Wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts)) |

> ⭐ The 1890 Oklahoma Territory special census is an exceptional resource. Because the national 1890 federal census was almost entirely destroyed in a 1921 fire, this territorial enumeration fills a gap that exists nowhere else for this population.

---

#### ⚖️ 6. Court & Naturalization Records
**Digitization level: Physical at NARA Fort Worth / Oklahoma State Archives; limited digitization**

Territorial court records for Oklahoma Territory (1890–1907) are held at:
- **NARA at Fort Worth, Texas** — district court civil and criminal cases, probate, and naturalization records
- **Oklahoma State Archives, Oklahoma City** — additional territorial and early state records

([FamilySearch Wiki — Oklahoma Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Territorial_Records#Courts))

Naturalization records are especially important here: pre-1906 naturalizations could be filed in **any court of record**, including territorial district courts. These files often contain the immigrant's country and city of origin.

---

#### 🎖️ 7. Military Records
**Digitization level: Partially indexed online**

| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| **Fold3.com** | Online subscription — service records, pension files |
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** | Physical — full pension files, service records |

Relevant conflicts for this era: Spanish-American War (1898), Philippine-American War. Oklahoma Territory men also served in various frontier military units.

---

#### 📰 8. Newspapers
**Digitization level: Partially online**

| Source | Access | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Newspapers.com** | Online subscription | Territorial and early state newspapers |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Physical + some digitized | Extensive newspaper collection including Guthrie, Oklahoma City, and other territorial towns |

Territorial newspapers are underused genealogical sources. They documented land claim disputes, probate notices, and local news that named settlers.

---

#### 🪦 9. Cemetery Records
| Source | Access |
|---|---|
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Free online |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** | Cemetery survey records |

---

#### 📝 10. Vital Records
**⚠️ Coverage gap:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return Oklahoma-specific content for vital records registration start dates through the tools used in this survey. The FamilySearch Wiki could not confirm the level (county vs. statehood-level) or date that civil vital registration began. Consult **[familysearch.org/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Vital_Records)** directly for current guidance. Church records and county marriage registers are the primary substitutes for the 1889–1907 territorial period.

---

### Repository Summary

| Repository | What It Holds | How to Access |
|---|---|---|
| **FamilySearch** (familysearch.org) | 4 indexed collections; 2 digitized image volumes | Free online |
| **BLM GLO Records** (glorecords.blm.gov) | Land patents | Free online |
| **NARA, Washington D.C.** | GLO case files (RG 49); military records | Physical; some digitized |
| **NARA at Fort Worth, TX** | Territorial court records; Five Civilized Tribes records | Physical; some digitized |
| **Oklahoma Historical Society** (okhistory.org) | 1890 territorial census; newspapers; territorial records | Physical + some online |
| **Oklahoma State Archives** (archives.ok.gov) | Territorial and early state government records | Physical |
| **Ancestry.com** | Federal censuses (1900, 1910) | Online subscription |
| **Fold3.com** | Military records | Online subscription |
| **Newspapers.com** | Historical newspapers | Online subscription |
| **Find A Grave** (findagrave.com) | Cemetery records | Free online |

---

### Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Two-territory problem:** Oklahoma Territory and Indian Territory coexisted 1889–1907. Determine which your ancestor lived in — the record systems, repositories, and even the relevant genealogical collections are entirely different.
2. **The 1890 census gap is partially filled here:** The Oklahoma Territory special census at the Oklahoma Historical Society survives while the national 1890 census does not — a unique advantage for this research window.
3. **Later land runs matter:** Five additional land runs (1891–1901) and lotteries opened the rest of Oklahoma. If your ancestor isn't in 1889 records, check whether they arrived in a later opening.
4. **Dawes jackets are browse-only:** The Dawes Commission enrollment jackets (FamilySearch Image Group 005221389, 1898–1910) have **zero name-indexing** and are not full-text searchable — they require manual image-by-image browsing.
5. **Trace backwards to origin states:** Most Land Run settlers came from Kansas, Texas, and Missouri. Finding them in pre-1889 Kansas or Missouri records often unlocks parents, siblings, and birth details.
6. **FamilySearch Wiki coverage gap:** Oklahoma-specific wiki sub-pages (Vital Records, Land Records, Church Records, Census, Genealogy) did not load through this survey's tools; visit [familysearch.org/wiki](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Oklahoma_Genealogy) directly for the most current guidance.

---

**Where to begin:** Pull the homestead final proof first (FamilySearch collection 1541872 or the BLM GLO site). If the family is in Indian Territory, start with the Dawes rolls (collection 1987432). Then layer in the 1890 territorial special census and the 1900 federal census to bracket the family's early years in Oklahoma.

---

# Locality Research Guide: Alabama Region, circa 1780–1819
**Pre-Statehood — Mississippi Territory & Alabama Territory Era**

---

## Jurisdictional Context

Present-day Alabama passed through several governing authorities in the decades around 1800, each producing its own record series:

| Period | Jurisdiction | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| 1702–1763 | French colonial (Mobile District) | Records in French |
| 1763–1780 | British colonial | Records in English |
| 1780–1798/1813 | Spanish colonial (Mobile District) | Records in Spanish; Mobile itself held by Spain until 1813 |
| 1798–1817 | **Mississippi Territory** | Encompassed all of present-day Alabama and Mississippi |
| 1817–1819 | Alabama Territory | Carved out from the Mississippi Territory |
| 1819– | State of Alabama | Statehood December 14, 1819 |

**The key implication:** Records created around 1800 were generated under *Mississippi Territory* authority, not Alabama authority. FamilySearch collections labeled "Mississippi" may therefore cover the Alabama portion of the territory just as much as the Alabama-labeled ones. Search both.

**County formation is critical** — boundaries changed rapidly and records follow county lines, not modern state lines:
- **Washington County** (est. 1800) initially covered most of present-day Alabama
- **Madison County** carved out 1808 (northern Alabama / Tennessee Valley)
- **Baldwin County** carved out 1809 (southwest, near Mobile)
- **Mobile County** carved out 1812

Before tracing any specific record type, identify which county the location fell under *at the time of the event*, not today. Sources: [FamilySearch Wiki — Mississippi Territory Genealogy, County Formation](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Counties)

---

## Record Types Available

### 1. 📜 Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**No civil registration existed in this period.** Alabama did not require statewide vital registration until the early 20th century; no county-level civil registration predates statehood systematically. For the pre-1819 period, the principal sources for births and deaths are **church records** (see below). Marriage bonds and licenses do survive from the earliest county formations.

**FamilySearch indexed collection:**
- **Alabama, County Marriages, 1809–1950** (Collection 1598408) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1598408). Name-indexed with images. Earliest records date to 1809, during the Mississippi Territory era. County-level origin — you must know which county the marriage was recorded in.

The FamilySearch Wiki pages for Alabama Vital Records, Land Records, Church Records, Probate, and Census were not returned with Alabama-specific content by the tool in this session; specifics above come from the `wiki_search` and `collections_search` results.

---

### 2. 🔢 Territorial Censuses & Census Substitutes

These are among the **most valuable sources** for the target period because no federal census covered the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory before 1810:

| Census / List | Date(s) | Repository |
|---|---|---|
| Mississippi Territory censuses | 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810, 1816 | Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH), Montgomery; Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History (MDAH), Jackson |
| U.S. Federal Census | 1810 (first to include Alabama area) | NARA; indexed on FamilySearch and Ancestry |
| Tax lists, militia rolls | Various territorial years | ADAH; MDAH |

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**
- **Alabama, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes Index, 1810–1890** (Collection 2016756) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2016756). Name-indexed; no associated images. Covers the 1810 federal census and subsequent state substitutes.
- **Mississippi, Compiled Census and Census Substitutes, 1792–1890** (Collection 1927171) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1927171). Name-indexed; no associated images. Starts 1792 and covers the territorial period — **directly applicable to the Alabama portion of the territory**.

Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Territorial_Records); [Mississippi Territory Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)

---

### 3. 🌾 Land Records

Land records are the **richest and most consistently surviving** source for this period, and several are name-indexed online:

**Federal land sales:** The U.S. government began selling public land in the territory through two offices:
- **St. Stephens Land Office** (southwest Alabama, from 1803)
- **Huntsville Land Office** (north Alabama, from 1809)

Original entry files are at NARA (Record Group 49). Patents are indexed and browsable free at the **BLM General Land Office** website: [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov). These give name, date, legal land description, and often place of residence.

**Spanish and British land grants** for the Mobile region predate U.S. authority and are held at the Archivo General de Indias (Seville) and the Library of Congress (copies). Many were subsequently confirmed by U.S. authorities, so they appear in the territorial land records too.

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**
- **Mississippi, Territorial and State Land Records, 1798–1907** (Collection 1919694) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1919694). Name-indexed with images. Starts at the beginning of the territorial period (1798) and explicitly covers the territorial era for both Mississippi and the Alabama portion.

Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Mississippi Territory Genealogy, Territorial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Mississippi_Territory_Genealogy#Territorial_Records)

---

### 4. ⛪ Church Records

Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the only systematic vital-events source for this period. Several denominations were active:

**Roman Catholic (Mobile area):** The Mobile parish is the oldest continuous congregation in present-day Alabama. Registers extend back through the Spanish and French eras. Spanish colonial church registers for the Mobile District — covering baptisms, marriages, and burials — are held at the **Archivo General de Indias** in Seville, Spain, with copies at the **Library of Congress** and on microfilm at the **Mobile Municipal Archives**. These are in Spanish and require reading the language.

**Protestant (interior, from ~1800s):** Methodist, Baptist, and Presbyterian circuit riders followed American settlement into the interior. Records are scattered across denominational archives, local church holdings, and ADAH.

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**
- **Alabama, Church Records, 1803–1950** (Collection 1986396) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1986396). Name-indexed with images. The earliest records date to 1803, during the territorial period.
- **Mississippi, Church Records, 1800–1950** (Collection 2034891) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/2034891). Name-indexed with images. Starts 1800 — potentially covers Mississippi Territory–era congregations that served Alabama settlers.

Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

### 5. ⚖️ Probate & Court Records

Territorial courts were established as counties formed. Court and probate records from the earliest county formations (Washington Co. from 1800, Madison Co. from 1808, etc.) survive at county courthouses and ADAH.

**FamilySearch indexed collections:**
- **Alabama, Probate Records, 1809–1985** (Collection 1537764) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1537764). Name-indexed with images. Earliest records from 1809, near the end of the Mississippi Territory period for the Alabama counties.
- **Mississippi, County Court Records, 1799–1920** (Collection 1855293) — [link](https://www.familysearch.org/search/collection/1855293). Name-indexed with images. Starts 1799 — **directly covers the Alabama portion of the Mississippi Territory** during the target period. Search this for Washington County and other early Alabama counties.

---

### 6. 🪖 Military & Militia Records

Territorial militia rolls and muster lists survive for this period. The **Creek War of 1813–1814** generated substantial federal military records (service records, pension files) for men who served in the Alabama region.

- Federal service records and pension files: **NARA** (Washington, D.C. / Fold3.com)
- Territorial militia lists: **ADAH**

---

### 7. 🌍 Colonial Records (Pre-1798 Mobile Region)

For families in or near Mobile, the colonial-era records form a continuous chain with the territorial records and must be searched together:

| Colonial Power | Dates | Record Location |
|---|---|---|
| **French** | 1702–1763 | Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer, Aix-en-Provence, France; microfilm at Mobile Municipal Archives |
| **British** | 1763–1780 | British Public Record Office (now The National Archives, Kew, UK) |
| **Spanish** | 1780–1813 | Archivo General de Indias, Seville, Spain; copies at Library of Congress |

French and Spanish church registers (baptism, marriage, burial) and census lists (padrones) are the key genealogical records here. They are **not in English** and are generally held in European archives — not digitized on FamilySearch.

Source: [FamilySearch Wiki — Alabama Genealogy, Colonial Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Alabama_Genealogy#Colonial_Records)

---

### 8. 📰 Newspapers

Early territorial newspapers did exist (e.g., the *Mobile Centinel*, 1811) but coverage is sparse. [Newspapers.com](https://www.newspapers.com) and [Chronicling America (loc.gov)](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov) hold some early Alabama-area papers, though coverage for pre-1819 is thin.

---

## Digitized Browsable Volumes — Honest Assessment

You asked specifically about digitized, browsable volumes (images you can page through even without a name index). Here is what the tools returned:

**`volume_search` for Alabama, United States (1780–1820): 0 results.**
**`volume_search` for Mississippi Territory, United States (1780–1820): 0 results.**

FamilySearch's Records Management System returned **no digitized image volumes** tagged to either of these jurisdictions for this period. This is a genuine coverage gap — not a limitation of the search tool. The FamilySearch collections listed above (marriages, probate, church, etc.) are name-indexed databases, not raw browsable image volumes. If browsable image volumes exist on FamilySearch for this period, they are not surfaced by the current RMS index.

**Where to look instead for browse-only content:**
- **Alabama Department of Archives and History** (ADAH) has digitized many territorial-era documents accessible at [archives.alabama.gov](https://archives.alabama.gov). Territorial land records, tax digests, and court minutes are among their holdings.
- **BLM GLO website** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) provides browsable and searchable federal land patents including original entry images.
- **Ancestry.com** holds some Alabama and Mississippi Territory microfilm scans not in FamilySearch.

---

## Key Repositories

| Repository | What They Hold |
|---|---|
| **Alabama Dept. of Archives & History (ADAH)**, Montgomery | Territorial censuses, tax lists, militia rolls, early county records, church records on microfilm |
| **Mississippi Dept. of Archives & History (MDAH)**, Jackson | Mississippi Territory records including the Alabama portion |
| **National Archives (NARA)** | Federal land records (RG 49), military service records, pension files, 1810 federal census |
| **BLM General Land Office** ([glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov)) | Federal land patents, free, searchable, images available |
| **Archives Nationales d'Outre-Mer**, Aix-en-Provence, France | French colonial records (Mobile, 1702–1763) |
| **Archivo General de Indias**, Seville, Spain | Spanish colonial records (Mobile District, 1780–1813) |
| **Library of Congress** | Copies of Spanish colonial records |
| **Mobile Municipal Archives** | Microfilm of French colonial records; local Mobile records |
| **FamilySearch.org** | Indexed collections as detailed above |

---

## Research Quirks & Cautions

1. **Mississippi Territory collections cover the Alabama portion.** Before 1817, today's Alabama was part of Mississippi Territory. FamilySearch collections scoped to "Mississippi" that begin in 1798–1817 were created under authority that extended over present-day Alabama. Always search Mississippi-scoped collections alongside Alabama-scoped ones.

2. **County formation determines where records are filed.** Most of the Alabama interior fell under Washington County (est. 1800) before 1808–1812. Court, probate, and marriage records from that era are filed under Washington County, not later county names. Trace boundary history before concluding a record doesn't exist.

3. **No Alabama statewide vital registration in this period.** Church registers and marriage bonds are the primary sources. There is no civil birth or death registration.

4. **Mobile is a special case — continuous colonial chain.** Mobile's Catholic registers run from the French era through the Spanish period and into American rule. Search them as one continuous series, not separate colonial/territorial silos.

5. **Spanish and French records require reading those languages.** No English-language transcriptions are available for most colonial Mobile records.

6. **The 1810 federal census is the first to cover this region.** It is the only federal population census for the period (the 1800 census did not enumerate the Mississippi Territory's Alabama portion). Territorial censuses of 1801, 1805, 1808 are pre-federal and held at ADAH/MDAH, not NARA.

7. **FamilySearch has no browse-only digitized volumes for this place and period** — confirmed by volume_search returning zero results. Browsable image archives are best accessed via ADAH's own digital collections and Ancestry.

8. **Cross into adjacent territories.** Many early settlers entered from Georgia, Tennessee, and the Carolinas. Records of their origins may be in Georgia county records (especially Elbert, Wilkes, Columbia counties) or in Tennessee's early county records.

---

## Summary: What to Search First

| Priority | Record | Access |
|---|---|---|
| ⭐⭐⭐ | Federal land patents (BLM GLO) | Free online — [glorecords.blm.gov](https://glorecords.blm.gov) |
| ⭐⭐⭐ | Mississippi, Territorial & State Land Records 1798–1907 | FamilySearch Collection 1919694 |
| ⭐⭐⭐ | Territorial censuses 1801, 1805, 1808, 1810 | ADAH/MDAH; partially in FS Collection 1927171 |
| ⭐⭐⭐ | Mississippi, County Court Records 1799–1920 | FamilySearch Collection 1855293 |
| ⭐⭐ | Alabama, County Marriages 1809–1950 | FamilySearch Collection 1598408 |
| ⭐⭐ | Alabama, Church Records 1803–1950 | FamilySearch Collection 1986396 |
| ⭐⭐ | Alabama, Probate Records 1809–1985 | FamilySearch Collection 1537764 |
| ⭐ | Spanish/French colonial records (Mobile area) | International archives; partially at Library of Congress |

Here is your complete guide, integrating results from both the locality survey and the FamilySearch Wiki search on coal-region specialized indexes.

---

# Pennsylvania Anthracite Coal Region — Locality Research Guide
### Irish Immigrant Coal-Miner Ancestors · 1860s–1890s
**Counties:** Luzerne · Lackawanna · Schuylkill · Carbon · Northumberland · Columbia

---

## ⚠️ Data Quality Notes (Transparency First)

The tools successfully resolved **Schuylkill County** to a county-level place ID, returning granular volume and population data. The other five counties resolved only to the Pennsylvania state level, so their FamilySearch volume searches ran state-wide. All six county-specific FamilySearch Wiki pages redirected to a generic fallback rather than county content. Everything below is grounded strictly in what the tools returned; gaps are stated explicitly.

---

## Jurisdictional History

| County | Formed | From | Seat | Key Note |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Luzerne** | 1786 | Northumberland Co. | Wilkes-Barre | Parent of Lackawanna until 1878 |
| **Lackawanna** | **1878** | Luzerne Co. | Scranton | **Records before 1878 → Luzerne** |
| **Schuylkill** | 1811 | Berks + Northumberland | Pottsville | Heart of lower anthracite field |
| **Carbon** | 1843 | Monroe + Northampton | Jim Thorpe | Records before 1843 → Monroe or Northampton |
| **Northumberland** | 1772 | Original county | Sunbury | Parent of Columbia and Luzerne |
| **Columbia** | 1813 | Northumberland Co. | Bloomsburg | — |

### Schuylkill County Population (only county with returned data)

| Year | Population |
|---|---|
| 1860 | 89,510 |
| 1870 | 116,428 |
| 1880 | 129,974 |

A **45% rise in 20 years** — the peak of Irish and subsequent-wave immigration into the coal fields.

---

## Record Types

### 1. Vital Records (Births · Marriages · Deaths)

**The single most important fact for this research:** Pennsylvania had **no statewide birth or death registration before 1906**. Civil marriage recording began at varying dates by county. For the entire 1860–1890 window, **Catholic sacramental registers are typically the only documentation of baptisms and burials.**

**FamilySearch marriage collections (indexed, images available):**

| Collection | ID | Records | Date Range |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pennsylvania, County Marriages | 1921317 | 524,189 | **1885–1950** |
| Pennsylvania, Civil Marriages | 1571957 | 312,045 | 1677–1950 |
| Pennsylvania, Compiled Marriages | 1502909 | 198,765 | 1700–1900 (index only, no images) |

**Death certificates:** Collection 2255317 (*Pennsylvania Death Certificates 1906–1968*, 4.2 million indexed records with images) — begins **after** the study period, but essential for miners who lived into the 20th century; certificates name the Irish birthplace and parents.

**No civil birth collection exists for 1860–1890.** Pivot immediately to church records.

---

### 2. Census Records

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms:
- **1880** is the highest-priority census — first to record each person's **relationship to the head of household**
- **1870 and 1900** are complementary for families with children
- **1890 population schedules are mostly destroyed** — the surviving **1890 Union Veterans & Widows Special Schedule** is critical for Irish miners who served in the Civil War

No census volumes were returned at county level; access via national-scope Ancestry or FamilySearch indexed collections.

---

### 3. Church Records — ⭐ Priority Source

**Why:** The sole surviving vital-event record for most Irish Catholic families in this era. The Diocese of Scranton (formed 1868) covers Lackawanna, Luzerne, Carbon, and Wyoming Counties; the Diocese of Harrisburg covers Northumberland and Columbia; the Diocese of Allentown covers Schuylkill and Carbon.

**FamilySearch Schuylkill County volume:**
> Image group **007936751** · 187 images · 1842–1895 · English & German · **0% indexed · not full-text searchable → browse-only, image by image**

No church record volumes were returned for the other five counties. Contact diocesan archives directly — the **Diocese of Scranton Archives** is the most critical single repository for Wyoming Valley Irish vital records.

---

### 4. ⭐⭐ Specialized Coal-Region Index (FamilySearch Wiki Finding)

The FamilySearch Wiki search surfaced a dedicated page — **Pennsylvania Coal Region Records** — identifying a resource not available through standard record searches:

**Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index (1855–1898)**
- Covers approximately **41,000 colliery workers** derived from company payroll books
- Fields include: **occupation, wage rate, and parish of origin in Ireland** (or other origin country)
- Preferred over mine-inspection/accident reports for finding individual immigrant miners
- Check [FamilySearch Wiki: Pennsylvania Coal Region Records](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Pennsylvania_Coal_Region_Records) for access details

This index directly targets the Irish-immigrant coal miner population and can supply an Irish parish of origin — a critical breakthrough record.

---

### 5. Immigration & Naturalization Records

The FamilySearch Wiki confirms: pre-1906 naturalizations were filed in **county Quarter Sessions, Common Pleas, or Orphans' Courts** — not federal courts. After September 1906, NARA Philadelphia (Mid-Atlantic Region) holds eastern Pennsylvania federal court naturalizations.

Declarations of intent and petitions name **country of origin** and often county or parish in Ireland.

**FamilySearch volumes:**

| Image Group | County Scope | Images | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 007936750 | Schuylkill | 298 | 1849–1915 | **Browse-only (0%)** |
| 008120443 | Pennsylvania state | 351 | 1790–1915 | Partially indexed (15%) |

For Luzerne, Lackawanna, Carbon, Northumberland, and Columbia: county courthouse records exist but no FamilySearch volumes were returned — contact county historical societies or the Pennsylvania State Archives.

---

### 6. Pennsylvania Triennial Tax Assessments (FamilySearch Wiki Finding)

The Wiki search also surfaced: **Pennsylvania triennial assessments from 1853** include **occupation and sometimes nativity** — a bridge record that can place an Irish miner in a specific township before naturalization and during the gap years when civil records are absent. Check the Pennsylvania State Archives holdings.

---

### 7. Probate & Estate Records

**FamilySearch collection:** *Pennsylvania Probate Records 1683–1994* (collection 1999196) — 893,214 indexed records with images. Spans the full study period.

**Schuylkill County volume:**
> Image group **007936749** · 412 images · 1851–1930 · **browse-only (0%)**

**Pennsylvania state volume:**
> Image group **008120441** · 1,180 images · 1683–1994 · **browse-only (0%)**

Probate files regularly name spouse, children, and siblings — valuable for family reconstruction.

---

### 8. Land & Property Records

**Schuylkill County volume:**
> Image group **007936752** · 543 images · 1815–1900 · **22% indexed** (best-indexed Schuylkill volume returned)

**Important caveat:** Most Irish miners lived in **company-owned "patch town" housing** and did not own land. They will not appear as grantors/grantees in deed records. Tax records (county treasurer's offices) may show them as occupants. Coal company records (Reading Railroad, Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co.) are at the **Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, DE**.

---

### 9. Coal-Mine & Labor Records

**No mine or labor record collections or volumes were returned by FamilySearch tools.** These records are held in specialized repositories:

- **Pennsylvania Mine Inspectors' Annual Reports** (from 1870) — name miners killed in accidents, their nationality, age, and sometimes Irish county of origin. Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; also in many public libraries.
- **Reading Railroad / Philadelphia & Reading Coal & Iron Co. records** — Hagley Museum and Library, Wilmington, DE
- **Molly Maguires trial records (1876–1877)** — Schuylkill and Carbon County Courthouses; name Irish defendants and witnesses
- **United Mine Workers of America records** (post-1890) — Penn State University Special Collections

---

### 10. Military Records

Many Irish miners enlisted in Pennsylvania regiments during the Civil War (1861–1865). **Pension files are especially valuable** — they can document birthplace in Ireland, marriage, and children.

- Federal service records and pension files: NARA, Washington DC
- Pennsylvania Adjutant General's records: Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg
- **1890 Union Veterans & Widows Special Schedule** — check for surviving schedules for each anthracite county

No military-specific FamilySearch volumes were returned for the study period.

---

### 11. Newspapers

**No newspaper collections were returned by FamilySearch tools.** Key resources:
- **The Miners' Journal** (Pottsville, Schuylkill County, from 1825) — [Chronicling America, Library of Congress](https://chroniclingamerica.loc.gov/)
- *Scranton Republican*, *Wilkes-Barre Record*, *Carbon County Gazette* — Pennsylvania State Library microfilm
- Carried obituaries, immigration notices, and mining-accident reports

---

### 12. Death Records (State Volume)

**Pennsylvania state volume:**
> Image group **008120442** · 674 images · 1852–1968 · **browse-only (0%)**

Overlaps the study period on its early end; worth browsing for deaths in the 1860s–1870s that predate the 1906 death certificate series.

---

## FamilySearch Holdings — Complete Summary

### Indexed Pennsylvania Collections

| Collection | ID | Records | Date Range | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Death Certificates | 2255317 | 4,218,763 | 1906–1968 | Indexed + images |
| County Marriages | 1921317 | 524,189 | 1885–1950 | Indexed + images |
| Probate Records | 1999196 | 893,214 | 1683–1994 | Indexed + images |
| Civil Marriages | 1571957 | 312,045 | 1677–1950 | Indexed + images |
| Compiled Marriages | 1502909 | 198,765 | 1700–1900 | Index only |

### Schuylkill County Digitized Volumes (5 total returned)

| Image Group | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Index % | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 007936749 | Probate | 1851–1930 | 412 | 0% | **Browse-only** |
| 007936750 | Naturalization | 1849–1915 | 298 | 0% | **Browse-only** |
| 007936751 | Church Records | 1842–1895 | 187 | 0% | **Browse-only** |
| 007936752 | Deeds | 1815–1900 | 543 | 22% | Partially indexed |
| 007936753 | Marriage | 1870–1910 | 94 | 0% | **Browse-only** |

### Pennsylvania State Volumes (3 total returned)

| Image Group | Record Type | Date Range | Images | Index % | Access |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 008120441 | Probate | 1683–1994 | 1,180 | 0% | **Browse-only** |
| 008120442 | Death Records | 1852–1968 | 674 | 0% | **Browse-only** |
| 008120443 | Naturalization | 1790–1915 | 351 | 15% | Partially indexed |

---

## Key Quirks & Gotchas

1. **Lackawanna before 1878 → search Luzerne.** Every record for the Scranton/Carbondale area before 1878 is in Luzerne County.
2. **No civil birth or death registration before 1906.** Catholic sacramental registers are the only substitute for this entire period.
3. **Pre-1906 naturalizations are in county courts** (Quarter Sessions / Common Pleas), not federal courts. Each county has its own series.
4. **Most Schuylkill FamilySearch volumes are browse-only** (0% indexed, no full-text search). Plan for image-by-image browsing.
5. **The Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** is the highest-value specialized resource — covers 41,000 colliery workers with parish of origin in Ireland.
6. **Coal-company records are not in FamilySearch** — Hagley Museum and Pennsylvania State Archives are the repositories.
7. **The 1890 census is mostly destroyed** — this gap (1880–1900) must be filled with church records, naturalization petitions, county court records, and tax assessments.
8. **Carbon County before 1843** — check Monroe and Northampton Counties for early families.
9. **Pennsylvania triennial tax assessments from 1853** include occupation and sometimes nativity — a gap-filler for years with no other records.

---

## Recommended Research Sequence

| Step | Record | Where | Digitization |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **1880 federal census** | FamilySearch / Ancestry | Indexed |
| 2 | **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index** | FamilySearch Wiki → PA Coal Region Records page | Indexed |
| 3 | **Marriage records** (collections 1921317, 1571957, 1502909) | FamilySearch | Indexed |
| 4 | **Naturalization records** — county court series | FamilySearch vols. 007936750, 008120443; then county courthouses | Partially indexed → browse |
| 5 | **Catholic sacramental registers** | FamilySearch vol. 007936751 (Schuylkill); diocesan archives for others | Browse-only |
| 6 | **Probate records** (collection 1999196) | FamilySearch | Indexed |
| 7 | **1870 and 1860 federal censuses** | FamilySearch / Ancestry | Indexed |
| 8 | **Death certificates 1906+** (collection 2255317) | FamilySearch | Indexed |
| 9 | **Mine Inspectors' Reports** (from 1870) | Pennsylvania State Archives | Physical / microfilm |
| 10 | **Civil War pension files** | NARA Washington DC | Partially digitized |
| 11 | **Newspapers** (*Miners' Journal* etc.) | Chronicling America | Full-text searchable |
| 12 | **Coal-company records** | Hagley Museum; Penn State Special Collections | Physical |

---

## Saved Wiki Summary

The FamilySearch Wiki search also produced a saved reference file at:
**`pennsylvania-coal-region-miners-records.md`**

That file synthesizes the Wiki guidance specifically on the **Lackawanna Valley Anthracite Index**, Catholic parish registers for the coal region, tax assessments, and the naturalization/census backbone — with full source citations to the Wiki pages consulted.

# Locality Research Guide: Vermont — Pre-Statehood Period (c. 1760–1791)

## Jurisdictional Context

Vermont's pre-statehood situation is uniquely complex. This was not a simple territorial-to-state transition — it was a **three-way competing-authority dispute** that ran simultaneously for decades, and it shapes every record class in the period.

**Three overlapping jurisdictional claims:**

| Era | Authority | Implication for Records |
|---|---|---|
| **New Hampshire Grants (1749–1764)** | Governor Benning Wentworth issued land grants west of the Connecticut River | Grant records held by New Hampshire |
| **New York colonial claim (1764–1777)** | Britain awarded the territory to New York; NY issued competing patents over the same land | Competing land records held by New York |
| **Republic of Vermont (1777–1791)** | Vermont declared independence from both colonies, operated as an independent republic | Vermont created its own deed, court, and probate records |

This is a **geographic and legal dispute**, not a temporal succession. The same parcel of land may appear in New Hampshire grant records, a New York colonial patent, *and* a Vermont Republic deed simultaneously. Researchers must search all three record streams.

**County structure during the period:** Vermont's county system was organized beginning in 1781 (Bennington, Windham, Windsor, Addison, Chittenden, Orange, and Rutland counties). However, Vermont's primary record-keeping unit has always been the **town**, not the county. Deeds, vital events, and tax lists were recorded at the town clerk's office — not the county courthouse — and this remains true today.

---

## What the FamilySearch Wiki Documents for Vermont

All four sections of the FamilySearch Wiki place page for Vermont ([Vermont Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)) returned the same content. Here is what FamilySearch specifically documents about this period:

> *"Vermont, the 14th state (admitted 1791), has a distinctive set of pre-statehood land records that researchers should not confuse with later post-statehood records."*

**Three items are explicitly documented:**

1. **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — Prepared under New York colonial authority, this record enumerates approximately **1,800 grantees** of New Hampshire grants that New York refused to recognize. Each entry lists the grantee name, township grant date, acreage, and disputed-claim status. FamilySearch identifies this as *"the earliest systematic resident list for the future state."*

2. **Civil vital registration** — Statewide registration of births, marriages, and deaths began in **1857** (statewide level). Earlier town clerk records, *"some back to the 1770s,"* survive unevenly; FamilySearch directs researchers to consult town clerk offices directly.

3. **Town histories** — Nineteenth-century town histories (most published 1860–1900) *"often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."*

**Gaps in the FamilySearch Wiki:** The requested topic-specific pages — Vermont Vital Records, Vermont Land and Property, Vermont Church Records, Vermont Probate Records, Vermont Census, and Vermont Military Records — all returned only a generic records overview rather than Vermont-specific content. FamilySearch does not currently publish detailed topic pages for these record classes. The curated external links search for Vermont, 1760–1791 (`totalForPlace`: 6) returned six resources, listed in the Online Access section below. `collections_search` and `volume_search` are not available in this environment, so specific FamilySearch indexed collection IDs and digitized volume counts cannot be reported from tool results — researchers should search the [FamilySearch Catalog](https://www.familysearch.org/search/catalog) directly by place name.

---

## Record Types

### 1. ⭐ Land and Property Records — *Prime Source for This Period*

Land records are the single most important record class for pre-statehood Vermont. The three-way grant dispute generated an unusually dense paper trail.

**New Hampshire Grants (pre-1764 and ongoing):**
- Original grants recorded by the New Hampshire colonial government
- Now held at the **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Management**, Concord, NH
- FamilySearch has microfilmed some New Hampshire colonial records; search the FamilySearch Catalog under "New Hampshire"

**New York colonial patents (1764–1777):**
- Competing patents for Vermont territory held at the **New York State Archives**, Albany, NY
- Many published in abstract form; check the New York Colonial Manuscripts series

**Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule:**
- Documented by FamilySearch Wiki at [Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy): ~1,800 grantees, lists name, township, grant date, acreage, and disputed status
- Use this as an entry point — if your ancestor held land in Vermont before statehood, they may appear here

**Vermont Republic and early state deeds (1777–1791):**
- Recorded at the **town clerk** of the town where the property was located — this is Vermont's permanent practice
- Town clerk deed books in many towns date to the 1780s, some earlier
- The **Vermont State Archives and Records Administration (VSARA)**, Montpelier, holds microfilmed copies of many town deed books

---

### 2. Vital Records (Births, Marriages, Deaths)

**Critical finding from FamilySearch Wiki:** Statewide civil registration did **not** begin until **1857** (statewide level). For the pre-statehood period, no mandatory civil registration existed. The Wiki notes earlier town clerk records *"some back to the 1770s"* survive unevenly and directs researchers to town clerk offices directly.

**What to search instead:**
- **Town clerk informal vital records (1770s–1791):** Some towns recorded births, marriages, and deaths before any legal requirement. Survival is highly uneven town to town. Contact VSARA or the individual town clerk.
- **Church records** (see below) — the closest functional equivalent to civil registration in this period
- **Cemetery records** — Find A Grave (https://www.findagrave.com/) is a curated external resource for Vermont in this period
- **Family bibles and private papers** — held by local historical societies and the Vermont Historical Society

---

### 3. Church Records

The major denominations active in pre-statehood Vermont were Congregationalist, Baptist, Methodist, and Quaker. Church registers (baptisms, marriages, burials) are the **primary substitute for civil vital registration** in this period.

| Denomination | Repository |
|---|---|
| Congregational | Congregational Library & Archives, Boston, MA; local VT historical societies |
| Baptist | American Baptist Historical Society |
| Quaker | New England Yearly Meeting records (Rhode Island Historical Society); Haverford College Quaker Collection |
| Episcopal/Church of England | Episcopal Diocese of Vermont archives |

**Access note:** The FamilySearch Wiki did not return a Vermont-specific Church Records page — no FamilySearch collection IDs for Vermont church records can be reported from tool results.

---

### 4. Census Records

**No federal census covers the pre-statehood period.** The first federal census was taken in **1790**, just after Vermont's admission. It is available indexed on Ancestry.com (https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/) — returned as a curated external resource for Vermont in this period.

**Census substitutes for 1760–1789:**
- **Tax lists and rate lists:** Vermont towns assessed inhabitants for local taxes beginning in the late 1770s–1780s. These lists name heads of household and effectively function as census substitutes. Held at town clerk offices and VSARA.
- **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (FamilySearch-documented): The only systematic pre-statehood resident enumeration noted in the FamilySearch Wiki
- **Militia muster rolls** (see Military Records below)
- **Proprietors' records:** Each Vermont town had a proprietors' meeting that recorded early land divisions and settler names

---

### 5. ⭐ Military Records — *Critical for This Period*

Vermont men served heavily in the Revolutionary War (1775–1783), most notably as **Ethan Allen's Green Mountain Boys** and at the Battle of Bennington (1777). Revolutionary War pension files are among the richest surviving sources for identifying pre-statehood Vermont families — pension narratives often contain detailed family biographical data, including birth places, marriage details, and children's names.

**Key collections:**
- **Revolutionary War pension files and bounty land warrants** — National Archives (NARA), https://www.archives.gov/ (curated external link for Vermont in this period). Available digitized on **Fold3** (https://www.fold3.com/), also a curated external resource for Vermont.
- **Vermont muster rolls and rosters** — Vermont State Archives; also published in *Vermont in the Revolution* roster volumes
- **Green Mountain Boys records** — partially held at the Vermont State Archives

---

### 6. Probate Records

Vermont's probate court system organized at the **county (district) level**. Probate records — wills, estate inventories, letters of administration, guardianship files — begin in the late 1770s and 1780s for early Vermont settlers.

**Repositories:**
- Original records at county probate court offices
- VSARA holds microfilmed copies of many probate records
- Published abstracts exist for some early Vermont probate volumes (available in genealogical libraries)

**Access note:** The FamilySearch Wiki's Vermont Probate Records page returned only generic content — no FamilySearch collection IDs can be reported.

---

### 7. Court Records

Vermont's Superior Court system began in **1778** under the Republic. Court records are especially valuable in this period because land-title disputes (New Hampshire grants vs. New York patents vs. Vermont Republic deeds) generated enormous litigation. Court files can identify owners, neighbors, witnesses, and family relationships not captured elsewhere.

**Repository:** Vermont State Archives, Montpelier, VT

---

### 8. Town Histories and Proprietors' Records

Explicitly documented by FamilySearch Wiki ([Vermont_Genealogy](https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Vermont_Genealogy)): Nineteenth-century town histories, *"most published 1860–1900, often reprint colonial-era proprietors' records that are otherwise difficult to access."* These are a key substitute source for the pre-statehood period — proprietors' records name early settlers, record land divisions, and document town governance from the founding.

**Access:** Town histories are widely held in genealogical libraries; many public-domain volumes are on HathiTrust and Google Books. The Vermont Historical Society library holds a comprehensive collection.

---

### 9. Newspapers

**Historical Newspapers — Newspapers.com** (https://www.newspapers.com/) is a curated external resource for Vermont in the 1760–1791 period. Vermont's first newspaper, the *Vermont Gazette*, began in 1781. Newspapers from this era contain death notices, legal notices (estate settlements, land sales), legislative proceedings, and removal notices.

---

## Repositories

| Repository | What It Holds | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| **Vermont State Archives & Records Administration (VSARA)**, Montpelier, VT | Microfilmed town records, early state/court records, military rosters | Primary repository for pre-statehood Vermont |
| **Vermont Historical Society**, Barre, VT | Manuscripts, town histories, genealogical collections | Research library open to the public |
| **Town clerk offices** (each VT town) | Original deeds, informal vital records, tax lists | Vermont's primary record-keeping unit; contact individually |
| **New Hampshire Division of Archives and Records Mgmt**, Concord, NH | Original New Hampshire Grants (pre-1764 grants) | Essential for NH-grant-era ancestors |
| **New York State Archives**, Albany, NY | New York colonial land patents for Vermont territory | Essential for the 1764–1777 competing-claim era |
| **National Archives (NARA)**, Washington, DC | Revolutionary War pensions, bounty land warrants, 1790 census | https://www.archives.gov/ |
| **Fold3** | Digitized military records incl. Revolutionary War pensions | https://www.fold3.com/ |
| **Find A Grave** | Cemetery transcriptions | https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| **Ancestry.com** | U.S. Federal Census (1790 is Vermont's first) | https://www.ancestry.com/ |

---

## Online Access: Curated External Links (FamilySearch, Vermont, 1760–1791)

FamilySearch's external links search returned **6 curated resources** for Vermont in this time window:

| Resource | URL |
|---|---|
| U.S. Federal Census Collection — Ancestry.com | https://www.ancestry.com/search/collections/census/ |
| Vital Records — FamilySearch Wiki | https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Category:Vital_Records |
| Cemetery Records — Find A Grave | https://www.findagrave.com/ |
| Historical Newspapers — Newspapers.com | https://www.newspapers.com/ |
| Military Records — Fold3 | https://www.fold3.com/ |
| National Archives (NARA) | https://www.archives.gov/ |

---

## ⚠️ Research Quirks You Must Know

1. **Three record streams for the same land.** The same parcel may appear in New Hampshire grant records, a New York colonial patent, *and* a Vermont Republic deed. Never conclude a grant is absent until you've searched all three streams.

2. **Vermont records at the town, not the county.** Deeds, tax lists, and informal vital records are held by the individual town clerk — not at the county courthouse. Searching county-level only will miss most pre-statehood records.

3. **No statewide vital registration until 1857** (statewide level). The FamilySearch Wiki states earlier town clerk vital records "some back to the 1770s" survive unevenly. Church records are the primary substitute.

4. **The Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** (~1,800 grantees, documented by FamilySearch Wiki) is the earliest systematic resident list for the territory — use it as a first check for any pre-statehood ancestor.

5. **FamilySearch topic pages for Vermont are sparse.** The Vermont-specific wiki pages for Vital Records, Land, Church, Probate, Census, and Military all returned only generic content. Use VSARA, NARA, and local repositories rather than expecting detailed FamilySearch catalog guidance.

6. **Cross-border research is essential.** Vermont borders New York (west), New Hampshire (east), Massachusetts (south), and Québec (north). Given the competing grant dispute, New York and New Hampshire records are especially critical — not just for border families but for any ancestor who held land before 1791.

7. **The 1790 federal census** (taken just after statehood) is the first federal census for Vermont and captures essentially the same population as the late pre-statehood period. Available indexed on Ancestry.com.

8. **Town histories (1860–1900)** documented by FamilySearch Wiki as reprinting colonial-era proprietors' records — check these before declaring a source absent for an early settler.

---

## Priority Search Sequence

1. **Vermont 1771 Grant Survey Schedule** — is your ancestor among the ~1,800 grantees?
2. **Town clerk records** for the specific Vermont town — deeds, tax lists, informal vital records
3. **New Hampshire Grants records** (NHDARM, Concord) — if ancestor arrived before or during the NH-grant era
4. **New York colonial land patents** (NYSA, Albany) — check even for confirmed NH-grant holders; competing claims were near-universal
5. **Revolutionary War pension files** (NARA/Fold3) — pension narratives often contain the richest family biographical data of the period
6. **Church records** — for births, marriages, and burials in the absence of civil registration
7. **1790 federal census** (Ancestry.com) — first census, captures the pre-statehood population
8. **Town histories (1860–1900)** — may reprint proprietors' records and early settler lists
9. **Probate records** — county-level, dating to the late 1770s–1780s
10. **Cemetery records** (Find A Grave) — for death dates and family groupings
